members.title: Frontier AI Regulation: Managing Emerging Risks to Public Safety
key_claims: Three factors suggest frontier AI development may need targeted regulation: models may possess unexpected and difficult-to-detect dangerous capabilities; deployed models can be hard to control and prevent from causing harm; and models may proliferate rapidly, enabling circumvention of safeguards
Industry self-regulation is an important first step but is likely insufficient; government intervention will be needed to create standards and ensure compliance
At least three building blocks are needed: standard-setting processes, registration and reporting (regulatory visibility) requirements, and compliance-ensuring mechanisms
Compliance options include granting enforcement powers to supervisory authorities and licensure regimes for frontier AI models, with licensing only warranted for the highest-risk AI activities

An initial set of safety standards should include pre-deployment risk assessments of dangerous capabilities and controllability, external expert scrutiny, deployment decisions informed by assessed risk, and post-deployment monitoring and response

Frontier AI models seem likely to warrant safety standards more stringent than most other AI models, such as avoiding large jumps in capabilities, adopting state-of-the-art alignment techniques, and conducting pre-training risk assessments
A compute threshold (e.g., models trained with more than ~1E26 FLOP) is offered as a simple, ex ante, objective initial way to identify potential state-of-the-art/frontier foundation models
Frontier AI regulation should be only one part of a broader policy portfolio and complement urgent efforts to address risks from current AI systems
methods: Conceptual policy analysis defining frontier AI and articulating three core regulatory problems (Unexpected Capabilities, Deployment Safety, Proliferation)
Proposal of three regulatory building blocks: standard-setting processes, registration/reporting (regulatory visibility), and compliance mechanisms

Comparative analysis of compliance options: self-regulation/certification, mandates and enforcement by supervisory authorities, and licensing of development and/or deployment, drawing analogies to other high-risk industries
Proposal of an initial set of substantive safety standards (risk assessments, external scrutiny, deployment protocols, post-deployment monitoring)
Appendix analysis of regulatory definition approaches, including a compute (FLOP) threshold approach, and a review of scaling-laws literature

members.title: AI Paradigms and AI Safety: Mapping Artefacts and Techniques to Safety Issues
Exploring AI Safety in Degrees: Generality, Capability and Control
Towards an international regulatory framework for AI safety: lessons from the IAEA’s nuclear safety regulations
key_claims: Improperly tuned AI subgoal-setting mechanisms may produce outcomes that conflict with human intentions, posing hidden risks embedded in AI's core decision-making mechanisms
Standardized international safety standards (as with the IAEA) can minimize discrepancies between national regulations and enhance the consistency and effectiveness of AI regulation
Transparency in AI's decision-making, especially subgoal-setting algorithms, plus human supervision and intervention, are key to ensuring AI stability and social acceptability

The IAEA's standardized safety standards and emergency response system offer transferable lessons for AI regulation, including standardized criteria, a neutral monitoring body, accident-response drills, and an international information-sharing platform
AI regulation requires international cooperation, multi-stakeholder engagement, and continuous updating to keep pace with rapidly evolving technological risks
Directly applying the IAEA's nuclear model to AI is limited because nuclear power and AI have different characteristics and risks; an independent, AI-specific regulatory framework is needed
methods: Comparative analysis of the IAEA's nuclear safety regulatory framework against AI technology standards and other regulatory regimes (EU, US)
Systematic review of regulatory documents (IAEA regulations, AI technology standards, EU/US frameworks)
Thematic analysis to identify major themes and patterns in IAEA regulations related to AI
Development of a three-pillar assessment framework (regulatory fitness, technical integration feasibility, regulatory efficacy) plus a case study of the IAEA's regulatory practices

members.title: Exploring Clusters of Research in Three Areas of AI Safety
key_claims: After filtering, eight clusters containing 15,197 papers were identified: three robustness, two interpretability, and three reward learning clusters
Robustness research is dominated by work on adversarial examples, with the largest cluster (#3735) containing papers almost exclusively on this topic
The two most-cited robustness papers are 'Intriguing Properties of Neural Networks' (Szegedy et al., 2014) and 'Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples' (Goodfellow et al., 2015)
Robustness and interpretability research grew rapidly during the second half of the 2010s, with robustness taking off around 2017
In interpretability, the United States leads but the European Union is a close second, possibly linked to GDPR's right-to-explanation provisions
Reward learning is a more awkward fit for the AI safety concept, with much work motivated by other considerations such as making robots more responsive to individual users
The United States appears to lead in every area, with China showing substantial growth in robustness and the EU producing a large amount of interpretability work
AI safety research may make up less than 1 percent of AI research overall

A bonus cluster (#54141) on AI risks and futures was found, including works like 'Concrete Problems in AI Safety' (Amodei et al. 2016), Bostrom's Superintelligence, and Kurzweil's The Singularity is Near
methods: Four-step cluster identification: (1) deriving three AI safety categories and keyword lists from three AI safety summary documents, (2) creating a list of 42 clusters meeting keyword (>=5% papers) and AI-paper (>=50%) thresholds, (3) manually screening cluster titles to a shortlist of 13, (4) sampling titles/abstracts to estimate relevance and discarding clusters under 40% relevant, leaving eight clusters
Manual screening of titles of 20-30 papers per cluster (10 most-cited, 10 core papers, up to 10 review papers) from the last five years
Estimating proportion of relevant papers via random sampling of English-language titles/abstracts with manual relevance evaluation, using a 95% confidence interval +/- 10%
Identifying foundational papers as the most-cited publications within each category's clusters
Plotting growth of papers over time by country/regional groupings
Informal sensitivity check using Chinese translations of keywords to check for additional clusters

members.title: AI Risk Management Should Incorporate Both Safety and Security
key_claims: Safety objectives typically focus on preventing harm a system might inflict on the external environment, while security objectives focus on protecting the system itself against harm and exploitation from malicious external actors

AI risk management must unambiguously include both safety and security objectives regardless of the definitions used, because mismatched/ambiguous definitions can cause important security considerations to be left out

Security is predominantly concerned with an adversarial threat model while safety has historically focused on non-adversarial/accidental harms, though adversarial threats are increasingly important for achieving safety objectives
Safety problems can often be framed as risk minimization over a relatively stable natural distribution, whereas security problems are inherently min-max games that are dynamic and lead to arms races
Ensuring security can be a precondition for maintaining safety, because compromised security-critical properties can cascade into harmful system behavior in the environment

Safety and security objectives can also technically clash, e.g., adversarial training and randomized smoothing improve worst-case robustness (security) while sacrificing benign accuracy (making models less safe to use)

The ineffectiveness of safety measures against adversarial attacks does not negate their value, since they still reduce accidental harm; performance should be evaluated against non-adversarial and adversarial threat models separately
Security mindsets are often marginalized in LLM technical reports, e.g., a keyword search for 'safety' in Touvron et al. (2023b) yields 299 matches while 'security' returns only five
methods: Introduces a unified reference framework comparing AI safety and AI security along four dimensions: objectives of protection (Sec 2.1), threat models (Sec 2.2), problem framing (Sec 2.3), and governance and liability (Sec 2.4)

Provides two deliberately non-overlapping taxonomies of representative problems — safety-oriented problems (safe usability and safe operation, Sec 3.1) and security-oriented problems organized by the CIA triad of confidentiality, integrity, availability (Sec 3.2), with extended versions in Appendices A and B

Conducts case-study analysis of frontier AI risk-management problems (combating malicious use; transparency/detectability of AI-generated content) to show where safety and security perspectives must be bridged and where they technically clash (Sec 4)
Draws cross-sector analogies and historical/policy comparisons (aviation, nuclear, medical devices, NIST AI RMF, NSF and DARPA programs) to argue for explicit accounting of both objectives

members.title: An AI System Evaluation Framework for Advancing AI Safety: Terminology, Taxonomy, Lifecycle Mapping
key_claims: AI models are only part of the broader AI system, so safety evaluation must move beyond model-centric approaches to system-level evaluation that accounts for environmental affordances and component interplay.
Divergent interpretations of key terms such as 'evaluation', 'testing', and 'assessment' across AI, software engineering, and governance communities hinder a unified approach to safety evaluation.
Narrow AI models are evaluated on Quality/Risk and Accuracy, while General AI models additionally require Capability evaluation.

Safety guardrail evaluation should focus on inherent characteristics across four attributes: generalisability, customisability, interpretability, and standards alignment, emphasising system-level (outside-model) guardrails.
Internal evaluation by AI Producers that excludes other stakeholders can reduce transparency and accountability, motivating a mapping of evaluations to stakeholders across the AI supply chain.
The taxonomy reveals a critical gap that existing evaluation practices may not fully grasp the complexity of AI systems, underscoring the need for an integrated evaluation framework.
methods: Harmonised terminology: a table of harmonised terms and definitions related to AI system evaluation (e.g., Narrow AI, General AI, evaluation, model/system evaluation, capability evaluation, benchmarking, testing, verification, validation, risk and impact assessment) drawn from diverse sources to enable cross-community communication.

A taxonomy for evaluating AI systems at both component level (non-AI components, data, model, safety guardrails) and system level (Narrow AI and General AI systems), organized around key areas such as Quality/Risk, Accuracy/Correctness, and Capability.

A mapping of requisite evaluations to AI lifecycle development stages and organisation-level stakeholders across the AI supply chain, adapting NIST's AI Risk Management Framework for a system-level perspective.

Conceptual reconception of evaluation terms (e.g., accuracy as task completion fidelity, correctness as system-level operational integrity) and a position-paper argument for shifting from model-centric to system-level evaluation.

members.title: Safetywashing: Do AI Safety Benchmarks Actually Measure Safety Progress?
key_claims: Many safety benchmarks are highly correlated with general capabilities and training compute, enabling safetywashing where capability improvements are misrepresented as safety advances.

Alignment-with-human-preference benchmarks (MT-Bench 78.7% capabilities / 79.8% compute; LMSYS Chatbot Arena 62.1% / 61.5%) are highly correlated with capabilities and compute and are highly liable for safetywashing.

Machine ethics depends on the benchmark: ETHICS has high correlation (82.2% capabilities) while MACHIAVELLI and Sycophancy have low or negative correlations, distinguishing knowledge-focused from propensity-focused benchmarks.
TruthfulQA MC1 is highly determined by capabilities (81.2% capabilities, 83.1% compute for chat), so misconception benchmarks are highly liable for safetywashing.
Scalable oversight benchmarks GPQA (77.7%) and QuALITY (88.8%) act as construct redundancy for capabilities and are highly liable for safetywashing.

Brier score is highly correlated with accuracy (95.5% language, 98.5% vision) while RMS calibration error is not (20.1% language, 15.2% vision), so Brier-based calibration is more liable for safetywashing.

Old-school adversarial benchmarks (ANLI 81.5%, ImageNet-A 97.9%) correlate highly with capabilities, while jailbreaks and gradient-based attacks (GCG, PGD) do not, so static adversarial benchmarks are more susceptible to safetywashing than dynamic attacks.

WMDP weaponization scores are strongly negatively correlated with capabilities and compute (Biosecurity -87.5%/-91.1%, Chemical -81.1%/-83.0%, Cybersecurity -86.0%/-85.7%), so weaponization benchmarks are not prone to safetywashing.
Bias benchmarks (BBQ Ambiguous -37.3%, CrowS-Pairs 28.5%, Discrim-Eval 33.2%) generally have low correlations and are not prone to safetywashing.
Capabilities score is highly correlated with training compute (Spearman 93.7% for chat, 96.5% for base).

Intuitive verbal arguments are a poor predictor of empirical correlations, so future safety benchmarks should report their capabilities correlation and be designed to be decorrelated from capabilities.
Increasing capabilities does not necessarily make AI safer, since it can improve some properties like truthfulness while increasing weaponization and malicious-use risk.
methods: meta-analysis
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Spearman correlation analysis
training-compute (FLOP) estimation
Brier score decomposition
benchmark evaluation via lm-eval-harness

members.title: The safety failures we are not instrumenting: a perspective on hidden safety-critical challenges in modern AI systems
key_claims: Safety should be judged by whether errors remain visible, contestable, containable, and recoverable
Hidden failures are plausible, distributed, temporally extended, and degrade correction mechanisms
AI safety is an emergent property of the deployment stack, not a scalar property of a model
methods: Perspective piece / operational synthesis and organizing framework
Five-layer integrity taxonomy
Practical control table with instrumentation indicators
Research agenda and design/governance recommendations

members.title: Key Concepts in AI Safety: An Overview
key_claims: Unlike tools used in engineering, modern machine learning methods do not come with safety guarantees, so many ML systems cannot be deployed without risking failure on previously unknown scenarios.
AI safety problems can be grouped into three categories: robustness, assurance, and specification.
Robustness means a system continues to operate within safe limits even in unfamiliar settings, e.g., by quantifying predictive uncertainty and alerting a human operator.
Assurance concerns whether a system can be analyzed and understood by human operators, addressed through interpretability/explainability techniques.
Specification concerns ensuring a system's behavior aligns with the designer's intentions; a poor proxy goal leads to misspecified, unsafe behavior.
Misspecification has already arisen in practice, as illustrated by YouTube's engagement-optimizing recommendation algorithm steering some users toward extremist content.
It remains uncertain when machine learning systems can be considered reliably safe.
methods: Conceptual/expository overview (issue brief / primer) introducing a three-category taxonomy of AI safety problems: robustness, assurance, and specification, adapted from prior work (Ortega et al.; Amodei et al.).
Explanation of robustness via predictive uncertainty estimation, illustrated with a satellite-imagery building-identification example.
Explanation of assurance via interpretability/explainability of black-box machine learning models.
Explanation of specification via goal/objective design, illustrated with the YouTube recommendation algorithm misspecification case.

members.title: Sociotechnical Safety Evaluation of Generative AI Systems
key_claims: Capability evaluation is the main current approach to safety evaluation but is critical yet insufficient; context determines whether a capability causes harm, requiring added human interaction and systemic impact layers

Three evaluation gaps emerge: a coverage gap (evaluations lacking for several risks), a context gap (human interaction and systemic evaluations are rare), and a multimodal gap (evaluations missing for multimodal/non-text systems)
Most identified evaluations cluster at the capability layer and overwhelmingly target text: about 75% of all evaluations target text output
There are only four publicly documented evaluations targeting audio and no evaluations targeting video were found
Even where evaluations exist they are not comprehensive: 83 evaluations of representation harms were identified, but only 17% cover binary gender and occupation bias and 60 cover text modalities only

Responsibility for evaluation is shared but differs by layer: AI developers have primary responsibility for capability evaluation, application developers for human interaction, and third-party/public actors are often best positioned for systemic impact
Evaluation is necessarily incomplete and never value-neutral, so it must be complemented by governance, post-deployment monitoring, and recourse mechanisms
For evaluation to be impactful four conditions must be met: relevant evaluations must exist, be conducted regularly, have real consequences, and become standardised and independent
methods: Proposes a three-layered sociotechnical evaluation framework (capability, human interaction, systemic impact) grounded in system safety / safety engineering principles
Synthesises prior risk taxonomies into a single holistic taxonomy of harm with six high-level harm areas

Conducts a large-scale review of existing safety benchmarks/evaluations applied to generative AI systems and releases an open evaluation repository, coding each by output modality, risk area, and evaluation layer
Maps the evaluation landscape and identifies evaluation gaps (coverage, context, multimodal)
Provides operationalisation guidance (mapping latent harm constructs to observable metrics per layer) and validity best-practices

Catalogs evaluation methods per layer (human annotation, benchmarking, adversarial testing; behavioural experiments, user research, passive monitoring; staged release/pilots, impact assessments, forecasts/simulations)
Presents a misinformation case study applying the framework across all three layers

members.title: Key Concepts in AI Safety: Interpretability in Machine Learning
key_claims: Interpretability refers to understanding the decisions of ML systems and designing systems whose decisions are easily understood, enabling operators to ensure correct behavior and get explanations for unexpected behavior
Many laws and institutions are premised on a right to request an explanation for a decision, which ML systems may be unable to provide
Deep neural networks are hard to interpret because they have far more parameters than linear models, each connected in complex ways rather than directly linking explanatory variables to outcomes
The term 'black box' is not quite right: researchers understand the math and can see parameter values; the problem is connecting millions/billions of values to concepts we care about
Saliency maps visualize which areas of an image led to a model's classification

Existing interpretability methods fall short, typically providing only one angle rather than a holistic view, and insights are fallible, require human supervision, and apply only to a small subset of application areas
The lack of a common, well-defined vocabulary for interpretable ML exacerbates these shortcomings, making it hard to measure progress
Until interpretable deep learning is achievable, the best option may be to use simpler, more inherently interpretable models whenever possible
methods: Conceptual/explanatory survey (CSET issue brief) introducing interpretability/explainability as a means to enable assurance in modern ML systems
Contrast of interpretable systems (rule-based if-this-then-that systems and linear models) against deep neural networks to explain why DNNs are hard to interpret
Review of saliency maps as a tool for interpreting computer-vision models
Review of feature-visualization methods that visualize how model components relate to high-level concepts across layers

members.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) - The Need for New Safety Standards and Methodologies
key_claims: The safety standards and regulations already in force for software applications are unlikely to meet the new challenges that AI will bring; a whole new set is needed.
There is a growing trend of handing over decision making from humans to machines via neural networks, raising real emerging concerns over transparency and lack of human control.

AI is a statistical approximate rather than a deterministic approach, and its black-box neural nets give no clear cause-and-effect relationship or guarantee against unexpected (catastrophic 'Black Swan') errors.

Neural networks are universal approximators that work best where the application has a high tolerance to error, and AI used in isolation should be treated with great caution where failure can lead to catastrophic consequences.
The well-established SIL process, with a complementary ALARP case, provides a suitable framework for the AI approach.
Implementation may be excessively driven by competitive marketplace needs while parallel safety research and standards may not keep pace.
Human specialists remain crucial and humans should not be rushed out of the decision loop for high-consequence applications such as nuclear weapon design and manufacture.
methods: Conceptual 'three technology revolutions' framework analyzing human control, transparency and complexity
Adaptation of Tegmark's three epochs of life to frame intelligence evolution and SAI
Qualitative analysis of neural-network mechanics (training/testing, weight adjustment, stochastic gradient descent, GPUs) versus deterministic software
Application of existing safety frameworks (Safety Integrity Levels/IEC 62061, ALARP, risk/SIL matrix) to AI
Structured Validation / V&V / Integrity / monitoring (RLI) checklist and residual questions for AI safety
Review of the Asilomar (Beneficial AI 2017) 23 principles, flagging safety-relevant ones

members.title: A Systematic Literature Review on AI Safety: Identifying Trends, Challenges, and Future Directions
Model evaluation for extreme risks
key_claims: Model evaluation is critical for addressing extreme risks; developers must identify dangerous capabilities and the propensity of models to apply capabilities for harm.
A model should be treated as highly dangerous if it has a capability profile sufficient for extreme harm, assuming misuse and/or misalignment.
Model evaluations should be embedded into governance to ensure responsible training, responsible deployment, transparency, and appropriate security.
Building comprehensive alignment evaluations is anticipated to be the most challenging part, requiring assurance across a wide diversity of settings.
Model evaluation is a necessary but not sufficient strategy for identifying and mitigating extreme risks and must be combined with broader organizational commitment to safety.

Conducting and reporting these evaluations poses four hazards, including advancing/proliferating dangerous capabilities, competitive pressures, superficial safety improvements, and harms during evaluation.
Frontier AI developers have a special responsibility to support this work, and should invest in research, craft internal policies, support outside work, and educate policymakers.
methods: Conceptual/position framework: extending the model-evaluation toolbox into two categories - dangerous capability evaluations and alignment evaluations - to detect risks from misuse and misalignment.
A governance blueprint embedding evaluation results into risk assessments and four decision processes: responsible training, responsible deployment, transparency, and appropriate security.
Specification of three sources of evaluations: internal model evaluation, external research access (via API), and external model audit by independent auditors.

A taxonomy (Table 1) of nine dangerous capabilities (cyber-offense, deception, persuasion & manipulation, political strategy, weapons acquisition, long-horizon planning, AI development, situational awareness, self-proliferation).
A list (Table 2) of desirable qualities for extreme-risk evaluations grouped as comprehensive, interpretable, and safe.
Survey of early empirical evaluation work, e.g. ARC Evals self-proliferation tests on GPT-4 and Claude, and DeepMind's 'Make-me-say' manipulation game.
Analysis of five limitations and four hazards of model evaluation, plus a deployment-controls table (Table 3).

members.title: Concrete Problems in AI Safety, Revisited
key_claims: Current AI safety vocabulary captures a range of real-world deployment issues, but an expanded socio-technical framing is required for a more complete understanding of how AI systems and safety mechanisms fail and succeed in real life.

In the autonomous vehicle cases, it was a lack of stakeholder engagement with the safety feature, not the technical function of the safety feature itself, that was deemed the primary cause of the accidents.
The Uber crash's official cause was the company's inadequate safety culture, which normalized neglect of established safety protocol, even though oversight functionality existed.
The Tesla crash involved overreliance on automation: the driver could interrupt the system but, lacking understanding of system limits, did not act in time.

Negative side effects are not only the actions of an AI agent; basic design and production choices (data, compute, labor) carry hidden human and environmental costs and reflect power imbalances between agents.
Scalable oversight failures arise when systems are trained on proxy or simulated objectives that overlook contextual factors, as with IBM Watson failing to adapt to new clinical situations.

Real-world AI failures are inherently systematic rather than contained in any technological artifact, and are rarely attributed to technological malfunction but to ineffective socio-technical interactions with users and stakeholders.

Analysts must consider errors in engineering practice, validate safety problems inductively through real-world case studies, and account for broader stakeholder impact rather than just alignment with technical design intent.
methods: Re-examination of the Amodei et al. (2016) concrete AI safety taxonomy, selecting three concrete problems (safe exploration, avoiding negative side effects, scalable oversight)
Identifying a real-world use case that fits each provided definition of the safety risk, then diagnosing the real-world nature of the challenge
Case study of autonomous vehicle fatalities (Uber Tempe crash and Tesla Autopilot crash) analyzed against NTSB findings to illustrate safe exploration
Case study of Netflix Prize / Doe v. Netflix and hidden production costs (data labor, facial recognition, climate) to illustrate negative side effects
Case study of IBM Watson Oncology Expert Advisor at MD Anderson to illustrate scalable oversight
Inductive thematic synthesis: surfacing recurring themes across the case studies for discussion

members.title: Key Concepts in AI Safety: Specification in Machine Learning
key_claims: Typical ML design forces designers to write an objective function that is only a simplified proxy of what they really want, and the more complex the task, the harder it is to find a good proxy

Specification gaming is a failure mode where ML algorithms achieve the specified objective with techniques disconnected from what the operator wanted, observed repeatedly in research settings (e.g., the CoastRunners boat looping and setting itself on fire)

The most concerning specification problems for policymakers are subtle, slow-moving misspecifications that only become apparent over long timescales or at large scale, such as social-media engagement optimization promoting extremist content and Amazon's resume tool mimicking gender disparity
A well-specified objective is necessary but not sufficient for safe AI; a system with a well-specified objective can still cause harm (e.g., malicious designer or non-specification failures)
Existing methods to address specification fall short: they are difficult or costly to implement, and none provides guarantees that no specification issues will occur
As ML systems become more advanced and deployed in more complex environments, specification problems may begin to bite without significant progress in methods to convey intentions
methods: Conceptual explainer / primer that defines specification and specification gaming for a policy audience using analogies (King Midas, principal-agent problems) and worked examples (CAPTCHA, mug-moving robot)
Three-level framework distinguishing ideal specification, design specification, and revealed specification of an objective function
Survey of three research approaches to avoid misspecification: learning from demonstrations, learning from human feedback, and inverse reward design
Real-world case-study illustration (social media recommendation, Amazon resume tool, organizational check-the-box training) to show pernicious misspecification
Policy implications and recommended diagnostic questions for policymakers

members.title: Landscape of AI Safety Concerns - A Methodology to Support Safety Assurance for AI-Based Autonomous Systems
Expanding External Access To Frontier AI Models For Dangerous Capability Evaluations
key_claims: Expanding external access can make evaluations more rigorous, reducing false negatives (undetected dangerous capabilities) and false positives (overestimated capabilities), and can increase stakeholder trust
Deeper model access enables higher-confidence evaluations but increases the risk of IP and security related information leaks

Security and capacity risks of expanded access can likely be mitigated through technical means (e.g. privacy-preserving access) and safeguards used in other industries (e.g. segregating duties, appointing a liaison)
The three proposed access levels correspond to the CoP's different standards for 'appropriate' access: AL1 to 'best practice', AL2 to 'state of the art', AL3 to 'more innovative'
Different aspects of access are interdependent but not substitutable (e.g. some vulnerabilities like backdoors are hard to detect with black-box access regardless of information provided)
AL2 is clearly within reach for frontier AI companies today because it is unlikely to pose significant security risks and remaining risks can likely be mitigated
Black-box methods have proved unreliable for detecting jailbreaks and backdoors, while white-box methods can uncover dangerous capabilities missed by input-output probing
The CoP states at least 20 business days is appropriate for most model evaluations, but in practice external evaluators often receive only about one week
methods: Proposes a taxonomy of access methods for dangerous capability evaluations that disentangles three aspects: model access, model information, and evaluation time frame
Reviews benefits and risks (rigour, stakeholder trust, security risks, capacity constraints) for each aspect and identifies potential mitigations drawn from technical safeguards and other industries
Classifies model access into black-box, grey-box, and white-box levels (Table 1)

Defines minimal, substantial, and comprehensive levels of disclosure across four information types: training data, deployment configurations, internal evaluation processes/results, and safety mitigations (Table 2)

Constructs three descriptive Access Levels (AL1, AL2, AL3) mapped to the CoP standards of 'best practice', 'state of the art', and 'more innovative', based on existing literature, expert discussions, and CoP definitions
Surveys publicly available evaluation reports, prior access arrangements, and existing standards (e.g. AEF-1) to determine current and innovative practices

members.title: AI safety: state of the field through quantitative lens
key_claims: There has been a significant increase in AI safety research activity since 2015, with the whole field seeing strong growth
Interpretability (with explainable AI / XAI) is the single most important growth generator for the field in the near-term
Value alignment is identified as the most important long-term research subfield / topic
There is a severe lack of research into concrete AI policies despite many papers on AI governance
The long-term utility of explainability is uncertain because such approaches lack guarantees for adversarial schemes and there are limits to explaining advanced concepts to humans
A considerable amount of AI safety research is not published in peer-reviewed outlets (e.g., pre-prints, blogs), and some organizations such as MIRI choose not to publish much of their work
Machine learning is the most frequently used tool/technique keyword in the research, followed by classification and deep learning
methods: bibliometric analysis
literature survey
descriptive statistics
database search query design

members.title: AI Safety Landscape From short-term specific system engineering to long-term artificial general intelligence
Introduction to AI Safety, Ethics, and Society
The Singapore Consensus on Global AI Safety Research Priorities
key_claims: Technical solutions for general-purpose AI systems are necessary but not sufficient for the overall safety of AI
Areas of mutual interest are research products and information that developers would find it in their self-interest to share widely even with competitors
There is broad consensus that current general-purpose AI lacks the capabilities to pose loss-of-control risk but expert opinion on its likelihood within the next several years varies greatly
State-of-the-art tamper-resistance techniques are very limited, often undone with only dozens of steps of fine-tuning on harmful data
Existing benchmark and audit measurements often exhibit weak internal, external, and construct validity
The science of evaluating propensities and capabilities of frontier AI systems remains nascent and current tests cannot rule out a given harmful capability
methods: Defence-in-depth framework grouping technical AI safety research into Risk Assessment, Development, and Control

Risk assessment via audit techniques and benchmarks, downstream impact assessment and forecasting, field tests and uplift studies, prospective risk analysis and structured analytical techniques, secure evaluation infrastructure, metrology, dangerous capability and propensity assessment, and loss-of-control risk assessment

Development via the safety-engineering framework of specification and validation, design and implementation, including robustness/adversarial training, tamper- and distillation-resistance, truthfulness, model editing, capability avoidance, and guaranteed-safe-by-design
Verification via robustness testing, quantitative and formal verification, interpretability techniques, and model organisms

Control via AI system monitoring and intervention, AGI/ASI control techniques (scalable oversight, corrigibility, containment, non-agentic guardrails, AI control), AI ecosystem monitoring, and societal resilience research

members.title: Review: First International AI Safety Report
key_claims: The source report is a ~300-page report from a global panel of experts selected by Yoshua Bengio, with 1168 references, summarized here as a 42-page AI-generated review.
General-purpose AI risks are categorized into three main areas: malicious use, malfunctions, and systemic risks.
Training compute has grown at roughly 4x per year since 2010, and experts predict models by 2026 may use 100x more training compute than 2023, potentially 10,000x by 2030.
An estimated 60% of jobs in advanced economies could be affected by current AI systems, with 40% in emerging economies, and women's jobs are roughly twice as exposed as men's.
Most notable AI models (56%) were developed in the US, creating dependency risks for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).
AI consumes 10-28% of data centre energy capacity, and data centres and data transmission contribute about 1% of global energy-related GHG emissions.

Loss-of-control scenarios are debated: AI may undermine human control intentionally or through misalignment (goal misspecification, misgeneralization, deceptive alignment), with potential outcomes ranging from human marginalization to extinction.
Current methods for training safer AI mitigate hazards but cannot reliably prevent unsafe actions, and adversarial training offers only limited robustness.
methods: AI-assisted summarization/review of a source report using Adobe Acrobat Pro AI Assistant (Kris Carlson prompting the tool)
Section-by-section synthesis of the International AI Safety Report, organized by risk categories (malicious use, malfunctions, systemic risks)
Taxonomy of the general-purpose AI development lifecycle (data collection, pre-training, fine-tuning, system integration, deployment, post-deployment monitoring)
Survey of risk-management techniques: risk identification/assessment, model testing, red-teaming, field testing, monitoring and intervention, and privacy-protection methods

members.title: AI Safety Landscape for Large Language Models: Taxonomy, State-of-the-art, and Future Directions
key_claims: The paper proposes a novel architectural framework defining AI safety through three perspectives: Trustworthy AI, Responsible AI, and Ecosystemic Safe AI

Unlike prior surveys that organize safety risks as individual topics, this survey integrates functional, ethical, and ecosystem-level safety in a coherent framework and systematically links risks to mitigation strategies

Ecosystem-level risks (content authenticity, misuse resistance, AI capability control, ecosystem-level alignment) consistently rank as high severity but low controllability, requiring coordinated governance beyond technical safeguards
Sycophancy correlates with model size and RLHF does not mitigate (and can escalate) it, suggesting it stems from training methodologies rather than particular systems
Very small amounts of poisoned data (e.g., as few as 250 malicious documents) can implant a hidden behavioral trigger/backdoor in models of virtually any size
Existing watermarking techniques are vulnerable to watermark removal attacks and spoofing attacks, and achieving completely robust watermarks remains challenging

Safety training has limitations: novel jailbreaks outpace model updates, safety training can degrade capabilities via catastrophic forgetting, and there is a helpfulness-safety trade-off plus an alignment tax
Guardrail approaches are theoretically insufficient to fully censor outputs and add computational overhead
methods: Literature survey methodology: querying scholarly databases (DBLP, Google Scholar) with predefined keyword combinations, then backward/forward snowballing, with two authors independently screening titles/abstracts under explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria (cut-off year 2025)
A novel three-layer architectural framework: Trustworthy AI, Responsible AI, and Ecosystemic Safe AI, organizing functional, ethical, and ecosystem-level safety

Formal formulation of AI Safety via two principles: Output Constraint (Principle I, prohibited output set Z) and Runtime Constraint (Principle II, runtime requirements R), with AI systems and AI pipelines defined formally

A shift towards data-based / data-driven safety assurance is necessary to address the characteristics of AI systems and the resulting challenges
A data-dependent safety assurance approach is mandatory regardless of the chosen safety approach, because AI behavior depends on both development-time and runtime data
Bottom-up assurance (pre-validating backbone models then fine-tuning) is impractical and insufficient because fine-tuning modifies weights and renders prior proofs/validations obsolete
Automotive AI safety standardization lags behind general AI standardization in data-dependency awareness and lifecycle consideration, while general AI standardization is itself still underway

Joint analysis along three pillars: AI safety research (Section III), AI safety standardization (Section IV), and AI safety regulation (Section V)

An implementation plan recommending the riders be field-tested first in an ACL workshop setting on a voluntary, non-peer-reviewed basis

members.title: The world’s week on AI safety: powerful computing efforts launched to boost research
AI Safety
key_claims: The rise of AI exposes a wider spectrum of harms (moral, social, political, economic), creating pressure to expand the scope of safety engineering, with 'AI Safety' used to encompass managing these wider harms.
Safety has historically been narrowly scoped to physical harm but has belatedly expanded to include psychological and then environmental harms.

Recognising the safety/security (accidental vs. malicious) distinction alone is counterproductive; safety hazards can emerge from security vulnerabilities, and the boundaries are even more blurred for AI systems such as deep neural networks vulnerable to adversarial attacks.

Societal harms such as algorithmic discrimination, racial bias, and targeted misinformation increasingly feature under the umbrella of AI safety, exacerbated by the scale, complexity, and opacity of AI systems, leading to responsibility gaps.

The AI development process itself raises 'upstream harms' (unfair labelling conditions, environmental footprint of training, privacy violations), so an AI model deemed 'safe enough' to use may still raise ethical and legal concerns in its development.

Among five candidate scopes, the authors judge the Comprehensive Approach (Option 5) the most promising, balancing focus on core physical/psychological/environmental harms with equity and treating other harms like misinformation as contributing factors.
Fundamental safety norms (starting early, whole-system mindset, through-life safety) endure under AI, and physical/psychological/environmental harm will rightly remain the focus of safety activities.

The authors are training a cohort of 60 PhD students through the UKRI Centre for Doctoral Training in AI Safety (SAINTS) to build multidisciplinary expertise for lifelong safety assurance of autonomous AI systems.
methods: Conceptual/position essay arguing how safety engineering boundaries should be reconceived for AI, tracing the historical expansion of harm categories from physical to psychological to environmental.
Argument that the safety/security (accidental vs. intentional harm) distinction is increasingly blurred for AI, motivating an integrated risk-based approach.

A scenario-based framing: six realistic AI-harm scenarios (A-F) are used to compare five candidate scopes for AI safety (Broad Scope, Traditional Focus, Refined Focus, Direct Causation, Comprehensive Approach).
Illustrative case analysis of the 2018 Uber autonomous-vehicle fatality (Elaine Herzberg) drawing on the NTSB investigation.

Novel training blend combining safety data with topic-following (TF) dialogue moderation data to improve generalization to new run-time risk categories
Ablations over prompt formats (catdesc, catlist, catlist+), response label source (jury of LLMs vs conversation-level vs WildGuard), refusal data, and stratified vs random subsampling

members.title: Building the Epistemic Community of AI Safety
Assuring AI safety: fallible knowledge and the Gricean maxims
key_claims: Safety claims justified by a safety case are descriptive (factual, about states of affairs) rather than normative claims, with the normative value judgments already made when safety requirements and the 'safe enough' threshold were set.

Safety claims are knowledge claims (justified true belief plus reliable-process justification), but they are fallible rather than infallible/certain knowledge because they rest on informal argumentation.

Even if a safety case aimed at infallible knowledge, the nature of AI-enabled systems (uncertain behaviour, open/unspecified contexts, black-box opacity, and large-scale consequences) precludes attaining infallible safety knowledge in practice.
Any infallible knowledge claim about AI safety is trivial, inheriting its certainty from a questionable premise such as assigning astronomical severity (e.g., human extinction) to an outcome.
Grice's Cooperative Principle and maxims can both structure the dialogue between communicator and communicatee and serve as criteria to evaluate the calibre of safety-knowledge exchanges.

Relevance is the most important maxim: high-calibre exchanges tailor communication to the communicatee's particular epistemic background while balancing quantity and quality and being communicated perspicuously.
methods: Conceptual/philosophical argumentation distinguishing descriptive from normative claims and analyzing safety claims as justified true belief with a process-reliabilist justification requirement and fallibilism
Analysis grounded in safety-case methodology and the formal-versus-informal argumentation distinction (drawing on Toulmin's account of field-dependent informal arguments)
Application of Paul Grice's Cooperative Principle and the Gricean maxims (quantity, quality, relation, manner) as a framework to structure and evaluate stakeholder communication
Illustration via a running hypothetical example (an AI-enabled ICU extubation-decision system) and imagined stakeholder dialogue exchanges (developer, clinician, patient, regulator)

Mechanistic Interpretability for AI Safety -- A Review
key_claims: Mechanistic interpretability aims to completely specify a neural network's computation, potentially as explicit as pseudocode (reverse engineering), distinguished by its ambition for comprehensive reverse engineering and strong motivation toward AI safety

Neurons are often polysemantic (associated with multiple unrelated concepts), which contradicts treating neurons as representational primitives; the superposition hypothesis explains this as networks representing more features than they have neurons via overlapping combinations

The linear representation hypothesis holds that features are directions in activation space (linear combinations of neurons), supported by much empirical evidence, though recent work identifies non-linear, multi-dimensional (e.g., circular) representations as counter-examples
Circuits (sub-graphs of features and connecting weights) are the computational primitive, and motifs are repeated circuit/feature patterns that recur across models and tasks, hinting at universality
The simulation and prediction orthogonality hypotheses suggest prediction-trained models like GPT may develop internal world models and simulate agents with potentially misaligned objectives

Mechanistic interpretability could promote AI safety (monitoring, anticipating emergence, substantiating threat models, alignment) but also poses risks: accelerating capabilities, dual-use harms, diverting resources, and causing overconfidence

Activation patching and related causal intervention techniques isolate the role of specific components by replacing activations, with clean-to-corrupted vs corrupted-to-clean directions revealing sufficiency vs necessity
This review is presented as the first comprehensive exploration of mechanistic interpretability research, complementing concurrent narrower technical reviews
methods: Literature review and synthesis of mechanistic interpretability research, structured around the broader interpretability landscape, core concepts/hypotheses, methods, a taxonomy/survey, AI safety relevance, challenges, and future directions

Establishing core conceptual definitions (features as representational primitives, circuits as computational primitives, motifs as universal circuit patterns) and formal hypotheses (superposition, linear representation, universality, simulation, prediction orthogonality)
Contrasting four interpretability paradigms: behavioral, attributional, concept-based, and mechanistic (causal bottom-up)
Proposing a taxonomy of mechanistic interpretability methods along four dimensions: causal nature, learning phase, locality, and comprehensiveness
Surveying observational methods (exemplar methods, feature visualization, probing, structured probes, logit lens variants, sparse autoencoders / sparse dictionary learning)
Surveying interventional methods (activation patching, path patching, causal abstraction, hypothesis testing such as causal scrubbing)

members.title: Multilayered review of safety approaches for machine learning-based systems in the days of AI
AI Sandbagging: Language Models can Strategically Underperform on Evaluations
key_claims: The paper proposes a new definition of AI sandbagging as strategic underperformance on an evaluation, with three conditions (strategic, underperformance, evaluation) and a distinction between developer sandbagging and AI system sandbagging
Frontier LMs GPT-4 and Claude 3 Opus can be prompted to selectively underperform on the dangerous-capability WMDP benchmark while retaining performance on control benchmarks
Both models underperform to a greater degree on WMDP than on subject-matched MMLU questions, indicating selectivity beyond just a subject area

A model (Mistral 7b) can be password-locked on a synthetic dataset to hide dangerous capabilities, and this generalizes to the held-out, expert-crafted WMDP benchmark, with full capability recovered when the password is provided
Frontier and smaller models can be prompted or password-locked to target a specific accuracy score (calibration), with most models tending to overshoot the target

A more capable model (Llama 3 70b) can be password-locked to emulate a weaker model's (Llama 2 7b) answers, producing a capability profile harder to detect than merely targeting a low accuracy; the Emulator matched the weaker model on 77.1% of questions versus the Targeter's 60.8%
Prompted models struggle to consistently emulate a lower capability profile in the zero-shot setting and only moderately improve with chain-of-thought prompting
Naive prompted sandbagging is easy to detect because models fail easy questions and succeed on hard ones, producing a flat accuracy-vs-difficulty profile
Trustworthy evaluations require more than black-box access; access to model weights and verifying the deployed system matches the evaluated one are needed to mitigate sandbagging

Password-locking via supervised fine-tuning with LoRA: training models (Mistral 7b, Llama 3 8b) on a GPT-4-generated synthetic dataset of WMDP-like and MMLU-like questions so capabilities are hidden unless a password is in the prompt, then testing generalization to held-out real WMDP

Synthetic data quality analysis using BERT embeddings, k-means clustering with the silhouette method, UMAP projections, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet semantic-similarity judgments

members.title: Inspect, Understand, Overcome: A Survey of Practical Methods for AI Safety
key_claims: A single safety mechanism typically targets only one insufficiency, so a holistic safety argumentation for complex DNN-based systems will in many cases rely on a variety of safety mechanisms
Effectiveness of safety mechanisms in mitigating safety concerns is assessed by safety metrics
Adversarial robustness is more of a security issue while corruption robustness (e.g., weather, Gaussian noise) is highly safety-relevant
Gradient masking alone is not a sufficient criterion for a reliable adversarial defense strategy, as shown by Athalye et al.
Modern neural networks tend to be overconfident in their predictions, motivating confidence calibration via methods such as expected calibration error and recalibration
Deep ensembles are the state-of-the-art frequentist approach to estimating neural network uncertainties
Deep compression can reduce network size for image classification by a factor of 35 for AlexNet and 49 for VGG-16 without any loss in accuracy
Adversarial training is still one of the most effective ways of increasing DNN robustness but is inefficient in terms of training time
methods: Survey/structured overview that first identifies categories of DNN insufficiencies and then describes research activities aiming at their detection, quantification, or mitigation
Dataset optimization: outlier/anomaly (out-of-distribution) detection, active learning, domain shift/domain adaptation, data augmentation, and corner case detection
Robust training: hyperparameter optimization, modification of the loss function, and domain generalization to improve adversarial and corruption robustness
Adversarial attacks and defenses: white-box and black-box attacks, universal adversarial perturbations, realistic/physical adversarial patches, and model-specific vs model-agnostic defense strategies
Interpretability methods: visual analytics, intermediate (disentangled) representations, pixel-attribution maps, and interpretable proxy/surrogate models
Uncertainty estimation: generative models, Monte Carlo dropout, Bayesian neural networks, frequentist uncertainty metrics, Markov random fields, and confidence calibration
Aggregation: ensemble methods (deep/snapshot ensembles, distillation, mixture-of-experts) and exploitation of temporal consistency
Verification and validation via formal testing (coverage criteria, differential/concolic/fuzz testing, SMT-based proving) and black-box methods (surrogate models, observers)
Architecture-level methods: CNN building blocks, multi-task networks, and neural architecture search (NAS)
Model compression: network pruning, weight quantization, knowledge distillation, and low-rank factorization for edge/real-time deployment

members.title: AISN #73: AI Safety Enters the Political Mainstream & Musk Loses OpenAI Lawsuit
AI for safety: rethinking risk in human-AI socio-technical systems
The First International AI Safety Report
key_claims: Autonomous general-purpose AI agents elevate risks of malfunction and malicious use by reducing human oversight, and are uniquely vulnerable to attacks such as hijacking via injected instructions
Developers understand little about how their models operate internally; current interpretability techniques are unreliable, can be misleading, and cannot yet provide safety guarantees

Harmful behaviours and unintended goal-oriented behaviours persist; safeguards can be circumvented via jailbreaks or simple modifications, and fine-tuning GPT-3.5 on only ten harmful examples can undo its safeguards
An evaluation gap persists: current safety evaluations are immature, and a model that passes current evaluations can still be unsafe

Existing quantitative risk-assessment methods (benchmarks) have significant limitations because risks depend on unanticipated use contexts and improving benchmark scores does not always reduce real-world risk
Adversarial training provides only limited robustness, and the advantage in attack/defence currently remains with attackers who can induce harmful behaviour with moderate effort
Training methods that rely on imperfect human feedback can incentivise models to mislead humans by obfuscating mistakes rather than becoming more accurate
Machine unlearning methods often suppress rather than robustly remove harmful capabilities, which can be reactivated
Competitive pressure in a high-fixed-cost, low-marginal-cost, network-effect market incentivises developers to under-invest in safety, risking a race to the bottom
Watermarks and AI-content detectors are useful but imperfect; watermarks can be removed by simple data modifications and detectors are prone to mistakes
The pace and unpredictability of general-purpose AI advances create an 'evidence dilemma' for policymakers who must weigh risks and benefits without a large body of scientific evidence
methods: Expert synthesis / literature review: a diverse group of 96 AI experts plus an international Expert Advisory Panel nominated by 30 countries, the OECD, EU and UN, summarising the scientific evidence on general-purpose AI safety

Enumeration of six technical challenges (autonomous agents, breadth of use cases, limited internal understanding, persistent harmful behaviours, evaluation gap, rapid global impact) and four societal/economic challenges to risk management

Description and assessment of risk-identification methods (taxonomies of hazards, participatory approaches, crowd audits, incident-tracking databases, adapted hazard-analysis techniques like HAZOP and bowtie/safety cases)
Four-layer risk-assessment framework: model testing/benchmarks, red-teaming, field testing (including human uplift studies), and long-term impact assessments

Review of training-based mitigation: adversarial training, RLHF and human oversight, scalable oversight (AI debate), safe-by-design/neuro-symbolic guarantees, hallucination reduction, interpretability-guided edits, and machine unlearning

Review of system-level monitoring and intervention: AI-generated content detection, watermarking, metadata/digital forensics, defence-in-depth, human-in-the-loop, secure operation protocols, explanation methods, and hardware-based monitoring

members.title: Safety by simulation: theorizing the future of robot regulation
key_claims: Emergent behavior is the key regulatory concern for mobility robots, and it arises not from autonomy, learning capability, or code unexplainability but from technological complexity coupled with near-infinite environmental variability and non-linear machine learning performance dynamics

Strong robot autonomy and continuous in-use (online) learning are misguided framings: robots will remain stable machines that execute code, and learning is a system-level lab process controlled by developers, not something happening during operational use

Explainability is a misguided focus for safety regulation because even fully transparent cognitions would remain unpredictable due to internal and environmental complexity, and robot injuries cannot be meaningfully contested

Both rule-based and performance-based regulation will fail to adequately constrain emergent robot behaviors; real-world and traditional testbed testing cannot generate enough evidence to demonstrate safety

Simulation-based regulation is necessary: regulators must supplement the real world with virtual twins and run massive numbers of simulations to verify safety across variable conditions and rare tail events

Simulation-based regulation represents a radical break in regulatory forms of knowledge and temporalities, enacting massive arrays of virtual futures to create a new, insurance-like probabilistic and totalizing knowledge type

The new simulation-based safety knowledge may destabilize safety politics (giving regulators unprecedented visibility and new policy horizons but risking code-driven law) and liability allocation (shrinking the development risk defense and pushing toward no-fault/strict liability)
methods: Conceptual/theoretical legal-regulatory analysis that surveys the regulatory 'playbook' (rule-based, goal/performance-based, design-process/management-based regulation, and liability rules) and argues why each succeeds or fails for mobility robots

Use of maritime autonomous surface ships (MASS) and their autonomous navigation system (ANS) as the primary technological case/mooring point to ground a generalizable discussion of mobility robot navigational cognitions

Critical reconceptualization of robot technological features, proposing a new typology (technical complexity, non-linear performance dynamics, environmental complexity giving rise to emergent behavior) in place of autonomy, learning, and unexplainability

Theorization of simulation-based regulation drawing on science and technology studies and Michel Foucault's forms of knowledge (inquiry and examination) plus an analogy to insurance/actuarial knowledge to characterize the new regulatory knowledge type

Analysis of downstream legal consequences using EU and Finnish liability doctrine (Product Liability Directive, development risk defense, negligence/Hand formula) and illustrative cases (Ford Pinto, Tesla recalls)

members.title: TAI-PRM: trustworthy AI—project risk management framework towards Industry 5.0
key_claims: TAI-PRM adds TAI requirements to existing ISO 31000-based industrial risk management methods to address the gap of merging trustworthy AI with risk management
E-risks are conditions/processes that may disrupt expected AI behaviour due to lack of consideration of TAI requirements including values, social, legal, environmental constraints

The framework extends failure modes with 11 ethical-based failure families spanning robustness, safety, transparency, accountability, well-being, human agency, privacy, data governance, bias, and users' values
Over 130 trustworthy-related failure modes were identified from literature review and industrial case-study feedback
Risk treatment uses the 4 T's (Treat, Transfer, Terminate, Tolerate) with stricter risk appetites for higher intrinsic-risk AI assets per the AI Act
The framework was validated in the ASSISTANT project with five academic and seven industrial partners and an accessible tool was built
methods: FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) extended with 11 ethical-based failure families derived from TAI requirements
Ethical risks (e-risks) concept integrated into risk management with drivers grouped as physical, social, data, user/system interface, and algorithm
RPN (S x O x D), Global RPN aggregation, and FMECA criticality metrics (Cm, Cr, ECN, ERCN)
RASP approach (Risk Architecture, Strategy, Protocols) on ISO 31000 with the 4 T's: Treat, Transfer, Terminate, Tolerate
Heat map / risk matrix construction linked to AI Act intrinsic risk levels using RPN percentiles/quartiles
Validation in the EU ASSISTANT project (digital twins for manufacturing) plus a supporting software tool

members.title: NeuroAI for AI Safety
key_claims: Neuroscience may hold important keys to technical AI safety that are currently underexplored and underutilized, via emulating brain representations/processing/architecture, robust sensory/motor systems, finetuning on brain data, neuroscience-based interpretability, and scaling cognitively-inspired architectures
Adversarial robustness is an unsolved, human-centric AI safety problem, and studying neural/sensory systems is a plausible route to progress

Extrapolated scaling laws project recording time to 80% FEVE of 3 hours in macaque V1, 8 hours in mouse V1, and 26 hours in macaque V4, placing good single-neuron digital twins at the edge of feasibility with current technology

In teacher-student simulations, matching internal representations (RSA) improves clean and adversarial accuracy, but adversarial training offers a more direct route to robustness; combining RSA with adversarial training gives only a small (up to 1%) boost, indicating a narrow direct path for neural data improving robustness

Whole-human-brain EM connectomics is currently prohibitively expensive (estimated ~$20T-59T), but optical microscopy with cell barcoding could plausibly bring a human-scale connectome within reach in under 10 years at under $1B

Visual BrainScores have remained stagnant over ~6 years (unlike other ML benchmarks that saturate), pointing to a lack of identifiability that prevents reverse-engineering the brain's objective functions

Recording technologies advance exponentially (electrophysiology doubling ~5.2 years, imaging ~1.6 years) but are dwarfed by AI progress (compute doubling every 6-10 months), so neuroscience remains fundamentally data-poor
NeuroAI offers a promising niche to enhance AI safety without dramatically increasing capabilities
An evolutionary curriculum plus a genomic bottleneck could yield AI that makes human-like rather than 'alien' errors and balances multiple objectives ('AI domestication')
The ~10 bits/s information-rate benchmark for finetuning AI with brain data is reachable by intracortical recordings, with fMRI within a factor of two

members.title: AI safety: necessary, but insufficient and possibly problematic
key_claims: The current global enthusiasm for AI safety is correlated with a non-technical notion of safety meaning that nothing unexpected or undesirable happens visibly
Interpreting AI safety merely as quality control (working as expected) is naive, since it just restates the well-understood necessity of software quality control
A stronger interpretation adds robustness to malicious actors (cybersecurity, red teaming), reflected in the US AI safety institute working groups on 'red-teaming' and 'safety & security'
Harms such as a job applicant rejected for reasons correlated with protected characteristics are misalignment/structural harms, not quality-control or security issues, and are hard to catch
Because AI safety as it stands does not mandate transparency, structural harm can be passed off as 'safe AI' as long as it is not patently visible
The US executive order's transparency (sharing safety results with the government rather than the public) is inadequate for tackling misalignment
AI safety debates hardly engage any of the three kinds of transparency, paving the way for developers to adopt opaqueness to comply with AI safety
The emergence of AI safety has influenced the EU AI Act so that 'safe' now refers to the AI rather than the safety of natural persons, deprioritizing latent harm to persons

The shallow notion of AI safety could allow intentionally harmful AI (e.g., racist predictive policing, discriminatory insurance pricing, exploitative gig-work wages) to be fomented under the label of 'safe AI'
Big tech's enthusiasm for AI safety suggests the emerging notion is not antithetical to their domination and could provide a veneer for continued profiteering
methods: Conceptual/critical analysis (opinion column) that unpacks the term 'AI safety' into three notions tied to non-technical usage: avoiding unexpected operation, undesirable operation, and visibility

Comparison of safety interpretations across policy initiatives: UK AI safety summit/institute, US White House executive order and AI safety institute working groups, GPAI ministerial declaration, and the EU AI Act
Use of a concrete anchoring example (an AI job-application rejection correlated with protected characteristics) to distinguish quality-control, security, and misalignment/structural harms
Distinguishing three kinds of transparency — technological (source code/data), objective-level, and decision-level justification — and relating them to GDPR Recital 71

members.title: TanksWorld: A Multi-Agent Environment for AI Safety Research
key_claims: The environment highlights three essential components: dynamic and uncertain environments, safety concerns for human and machine teams, and complex tasks with competing objectives.
Existing AI Safety Gridworlds present only minimalistic examples and consist of only a single AI-controlled entity, making them unsuitable for studying human-machine teaming.
Parameterizing communication range can alter scenarios from full observability to partial observability, and distributional shifts force policies to cope with unreliable communications.
Neutral tanks present collateral damage risk, addressing the concrete AI safety problem of avoiding unintended consequences.
The competitive, dynamic nature forces agents to trade off task performance against safety objectives, supporting exploration of multi-objective optimization.
This is a work in progress; the paper introduces research objectives and the learning environment, with baseline performance metrics deferred to future work.
methods: AI Safety TanksWorld: a team-based N vs. N tanks battle environment built largely from Unity-distributed assets, where one team aims to defeat the other while avoiding unintended consequences like losing teammates or collateral damage.
State representation as a tank-relative 128x128 4-channel image (allies, visible threats, neutral tanks, obstacles), rotated/translated relative to each tank's position and heading.
Continuous action space with three actions per agent: velocity (forward/reverse), turning (left/right), and shooting (yes/no), all in range -1 to 1 with rate-limited shooting.
Active sensing and teamwork model: each tank has partial observability, with transitive communication between allies within a parameterized communication radius to share observed threats.
Parameterization of the environment via communication range, number of neutral tanks and obstacles, and control policies of teammates to emphasize different research challenges.
Human surrogate policies for teammates learned via behavior cloning from human demonstrations (or explicit behavior modeling) to study human-machine teaming.
Separate reward metrics for allied, neutral, and opponent kills, allowing flexible reward/constraint definitions across performance-risk trade-offs.

members.title: Actionable Guidance for High-Consequence AI Risk Management: Towards Standards Addressing AI Catastrophic Risks
key_claims: Treatment of large-scale and catastrophic AI risks in the AI RMF to date had been framed more as challenges than as detailed actionable guidance, motivating proactively drafted supplementary guidance.

Advanced/multi-purpose AI systems (e.g., BERT, CLIP, GPT-3, DALL-E 2, PaLM) have qualitatively distinct properties such as application to many sectors at once and emergent properties, creating catastrophic risks like correlated robustness failures across multiple high-stakes domains.

Preventing catastrophe is part of preventing unfair outcomes, because the effects of catastrophe often fall disproportionately on disadvantaged people; protecting human rights is a critical component of mitigating societal and catastrophic risks.

Organizations should identify not only intended uses but also other beneficial uses and misuse/abuse cases (using threat modeling, red teaming, resources like MITRE ATLAS), and incorporate them into harms modeling and risk assessments.

The proposed impact-rating scale adds explicit catastrophic-risk factors to a NIST SP 800-30-derived scale, listing factors such as correlated robustness failures, other systemic risks, correlated bias, many high-impact uses/misuses beyond intended use, and large harms from mis-specified goals.

NIST should provide an AI RMF Profile specifically for cutting-edge, increasingly multi-purpose or general-purpose AI (including foundation models) to target a small number of high-risk systems while minimizing costs for narrower AI.

Upstream developers of foundation-model platforms and downstream developers building end-use applications should hold differentiated AI RMF responsibilities matched to their information and capability in the value chain.

Specific safety/control measures are recommended for high-risk attributes such as recursive self-improvement via code generation; measures include staged/structured-access release, off-switch/kill-switch mechanisms, incremental compute scaling with red-team probing, and least-privilege design.

The work recommends roadmap items for later AI RMF versions, including a comprehensive set of governance mechanisms, objectives-specification (alignment) characterization and measurement, generality assessment, recursive-improvement-potential measurement, and other AI safety measurement tools.
methods: Proactive drafting of small, modular pieces of actionable guidance for AI RMF 1.0, mined from prior submissions to NIST (e.g., NIST 2021b, CLTC 2022), discussions with colleagues, and review of relevant literature

Definition and application of explicit inclusion criteria to decide whether draft guidance belongs in AI RMF 1.0 vs. a roadmap for later versions: actionable/clear, best-practice/citable, ERM-compatible, lifecycle-compatible, standards/regulation-compatible, measurable or documentable, small/tractable, modular, low downside, and helping NIST address its legislative mandate
Adaptation and mapping of guidance onto AI RMF core functions (Map, Measure, Manage, Govern) and specific AI RMF subcategories (e.g., Map 1.1, Map 5.1, Manage 1.3)

Adaptation of existing standards and resources, including NIST SP 800-30 (an impact-rating scale closely following Table H-3), NIST Cybersecurity and Privacy Frameworks, cybersecurity 'misuse/abuse case' and threat-modeling concepts, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the UDHR, the OECD classification framework, the draft EU AI Act, and the AI Incident Database CSET taxonomy

members.title: A review on AI Safety in highly automated driving
key_claims: For many AI systems, especially neural-network-based ones, classical safety analysis methods can hardly be applied and current standards do not address developing safe AI systems, so validation, verification, and testing must be considered.

ML-based systems cannot fully satisfy current safety standards such as ISO26262 (e.g., ML can create new hazards from human interaction, has distinct fault/failure modes, depends on inherently incomplete training data, and ANN black-box character violates hierarchical decomposition).

Two distinct classes of approaches were identified: established (classical) methods referring to published standards or well-established concepts from outside ML/AI, and newly developed approaches tailored to ML/AI.

Robustness against adversarial attacks is a key new concern: imperceptible input perturbations can cause neural-network classifiers to misclassify adversarial examples, and formal verification of neural networks is NP-complete and difficult.

Value alignment is central to validation of ML systems; reward hacking (e.g., the cleaning robot deactivating its perception to avoid seeing messes) shows training can optimize the objective without solving the real problem, with inverse reinforcement learning a promising remedy.

The term 'AI Safety' is not yet well-established, appearing only 12 times in the searched literature while other phrases like 'AI Testing' or 'Safety AND Artificial Intelligence' appear more often, even as AI Safety publications trend upward.
Findings from the aerospace sector, which has long faced verification and validation of AI systems, should be taken into account as guidance for developing safe AI systems in the automotive sector.
Splitting the safety assessment of AI systems into the separate tasks of validation, verification, and testing is seen as a promising reference point for future development.

An original conceptual taxonomy of 77 codes organized into five domains: risk factors governed, harms addressed, governance strategies, incentives for compliance, and application domains addressed
