Manual and semi-automated collection of candidate documents from official, unofficial, and informal sources, followed by human screening against the scoping definition
Annotation workflow using a custom-built Airtable interface where annotators generate summaries and apply thematic codes after reading each instrument in full
Dual annotation and validation process: an initial annotator codes the instrument and a second annotator (validator) reviews it and reconciles disagreements
Inter-rater reliability assessment on 21 instruments using two annotator-validator pairs, computing Guilford's g and Gwet's AC1
Public distribution via a web-based interface (https://agora.eto.tech) and a bulk dataset
Planned experimentation with large language models to summarize and annotate instruments and integration with regulatory APIs

members.title: Frontier AI regulation: what form should it take?
key_claims: Current regulatory efforts for frontier AI are fragmented and reactive, lacking provisions to address evolving risks
AI regulation should adopt a security-first, risk-based governance model with proactive compliance and coordinated global oversight rather than purely idealistic ethical frameworks

Cryptographic techniques (homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs) can enable privacy-preserving compliance verification but are computationally intensive and can be exploited for illicit anonymity absent a standardized identity management system
Existing explainability methods such as LIME and SHAP provide only limited traceability/interpretability for complex AI systems, necessitating more advanced approaches
A pragmatic, decentralised regulatory blueprint is needed because most countries do not follow EU ideals, balancing technological advancement with security enforcement
AI supply chain interdependencies create cascading cybersecurity risks where data poisoning in a foundational model propagates to downstream services
Regulatory frameworks should incorporate environmental sustainability metrics given the large carbon and water footprints of generative AI models
International governance proposals include a 'World AI Organisation' akin to the Paris Agreement to provide unified global oversight
methods: comparative policy analysis
interdisciplinary synthesis (cybersecurity, legal, computational risk)
cryptographic technique review
conceptual framework / blueprint development

members.title: Common guideposts to promote interoperability in AI risk management
Taming Artificial Intelligence: A Theory of Control-Accountability Alignment among AI Developers and Users
Observe, inspect, modify: Three conditions for generative AI governance
Towards Responsible AI: Exploring AI Frameworks, Ethical Dimensions and Regulations
On the Development of AI Governance Frameworks
Acceptable Risks in Europe’s Proposed AI Act: Reasonableness and Other Principles for Deciding How Much Risk Management Is Enough
key_claims: The Commission's requirement to reduce risks AFAP is neither workable nor consistent with the Act's stated goals, creating too indeterminate a risk management obligation inconsistent with proportionality.
The very uncertainty of AFAP may perversely encourage regulatees to fudge acceptability judgments without principled justification, which is a poor formula for trustworthiness.
The Parliament's amendments, which introduce reasonableness and cost-benefit considerations, would make risk management more proportionate and more principled, without sacrificing trustworthiness.
Reasonableness permits principled, transparent weighing of cost-benefit ratios, risk-benefit ratios, and materiality of risk, allowing context-sensitive acceptability judgments.
AFAP combined with a vague 'state of the art' cedes control over public-policy matters to technical standards bodies that lack the legitimacy and expertise to make fundamental-rights value judgments.
Risk-acceptability judgments are unavoidably value-laden and political, and require a firm foundation of civic legitimacy via regulator guidance and meaningful stakeholder input.
ALARP, which the Commission rejected for medical devices, may be a workable 'third way' compromise criterion that embeds a precautionary approach and is well understood by risk managers.
methods: Doctrinal/comparative legal analysis comparing the Commission's original Article 9 text with the Council's and Parliament's proposed amendments to risk management and risk acceptability provisions
Historical/contextual analysis of the Commission's narrow interpretation of AFAP in European medical devices regulation (e.g. EN ISO 14971, ALARP-to-AFAP shift) to illustrate its problems
Drawing on negligence-law jurisprudence (the four-factor reasonableness test) and Principles of European Tort Law to explain what 'reasonableness' in risk-acceptability judgments entails
Normative/regulatory-theory argument about civic legitimacy, the precautionary principle, standards bodies, and the need for stakeholder and regulator involvement

members.title: Responsible AI Governance: A Systematic Literature Review
key_claims: 61 relevant articles on AI Governance were identified and analysed, of which only 5 provided complete responses to all 3W1H questions
There is a disproportionate emphasis on 'how' AI should be governed (20 of 61 studies) while neglecting who is responsible and at what lifecycle stage
Not a single study out of 61 mentioned the human pillar as something to be governed; data and systems receive more attention than processes and humans
The highest number of AI governance solutions (19) are categorised under organisational-level governance
Ethical challenges such as fairness, transparency, privacy, and trust are the most discussed challenges of AI governance in the literature
Healthcare and robotics are the most common targeted AI application domains, with healthcare targeted in 10 studies and robotics in three, while 25 studies did not specify a domain
methods: Systematic literature review (SLR) following Kitchenham et al. guidelines, extended to include non-empirical and secondary studies given limited empirical work on AI governance

Search strategy using keywords ((AI OR artificial intelligence) AND (governance)) across Google Scholar, Scopus, Science Direct, IEEE, and ACM for English papers 2013-2023, with inclusion/exclusion criteria
Screening and selection pipeline (2918 papers screened, 225 selected, then 61 final studies) using forward and backward snowballing
3W1H (Who, What, When, How) analytical approach applied via thematic analysis to the 61 selected studies
Categorisation of stakeholders and governance artefacts under five AI governance levels (team, organisation, industry, national, international), inspired by Lu et al.'s pattern catalogue

members.title: AI governance: a systematic literature review
key_claims: The study analyzed 28 selected articles to provide a foundation for understanding different facets of AI governance, using four questions: who is accountable, what is governed, when governance occurs, and how it is implemented
Of the 28 selected papers, 20 were deemed Good quality, 8 were Fair quality, and 0 were Poor quality
Studies on governance solutions primarily focused on just one or two ethical AI principles, most frequently fairness followed by privacy
Only three studies (A2, A11, A13) answered all four questions (who, what, when, and how)
The highest number (7) of AI governance solutions fall under organizational-level governance, while none fall under team-level or national-level governance
Key challenges identified include less attention to ethical and responsible AI principles, lack of human involvement, and inadequacy of current governance approaches
Governance solutions and stakeholders are categorized under five levels of governance: team-level, organization-level, industry-level, national-level, and international-level
methods: Systematic literature review (SLR) following Kitchenham et al. guidelines, with planning, conducting the review, and reporting phases
Search of Scopus and Google Scholar using keywords 'AI', 'artificial intelligence', and 'governance' for 2013-2023, returning 2918 papers
Multi-stage selection: inclusion/exclusion criteria on abstracts and full papers, test-retest expert review in multiple rounds, and forward/backward snowballing, yielding 28 final papers
Quality assessment using a five-question criteria from Liu et al., scoring each question 0/0.5/1 and categorizing studies as Good, Fair, or Poor
Data extraction into an Excel spreadsheet capturing demographic and content data, with manual coding by the first author cross-checked in weekly meetings
Thematic analysis answering four questions (Who, What, When, How) mapped to the four pillars (humans, data, systems, processes) from Zowghi and da Rimini
Categorization of stakeholders and governance solutions under five governance levels (team, organization, industry, national, international) following Lu et al.

members.title: Computing Power and the Governance of Artificial Intelligence
key_claims: AI-relevant compute is detectable, excludable, and quantifiable, and is produced via an extremely concentrated supply chain
Compute governance can enhance the three capacities of visibility, allocation, and enforcement
Training compute for notable ML models has doubled roughly every six months, growing by a factor of 350 million over 13 years
Deployment-only regulation is inadequate; development must also be regulated via compute
The AI chip supply chain is dominated by a small number of actors (TSMC, ASML, NVIDIA)
Poorly scoped compute governance risks privacy, information leakage, economic harm, and centralization of power
Algorithmic and hardware progress erodes compute governance effectiveness over time
methods: Conceptual policy analysis of compute's governable properties
Taxonomy of governance capacities (visibility, allocation, enforcement)
Illustrative policy mechanism design and critique
Empirical compute-trend and scaling-law synthesis from prior data
Compute-uranium analogy and risk/guardrail analysis

members.title: Local AI Governance: Addressing Model Safety and Policy Challenges Posed by Decentralized AI
The governance of artificial intelligence in Canada: Findings and opportunities from a review of 84 AI governance initiatives
On the Limitations of Compute Thresholds as a Governance Strategy
key_claims: Compute thresholds as currently implemented are shortsighted and likely to fail to mitigate risk because the relationship between compute and risk is highly uncertain and rapidly changing.
The choice of 10^26 and 10^25 FLOP thresholds has not been scientifically justified in any policy implementing them.

Compute thresholds are largely precautionary: almost no models currently deployed in the wild meet the criteria, so the emphasis is on hypothetical future risks rather than auditing currently deployed models.
Smaller models are becoming increasingly performant and routinely outperform much larger models, driven by data quality, optimization, and architecture rather than raw FLOP.

Training FLOP fails to account for inference-time compute enhancements, which can impart large performance gains (estimated 5x to 20x of base post-training performance) and dramatically change a model's risk profile.
FLOP says nothing about end performance or safety alignment; two models with identical FLOP can present very different risk (e.g., one with safety alignment, one without).

Existing policies leave FLOP underspecified, creating exploitable loopholes (lifecycle tracking, Mixture of Experts, ensembles, system/agent-level risk, modalities, quantization), a lesson in Goodhart's Law.

We are not good at predicting which downstream capabilities emerge at different scales; scaling laws reliably hold mainly for pre-training loss, not downstream performance, undermining the scientific basis for thresholds.

The compute-performance distribution is one of the most misbehaved and rapidly changing distributions, so hard-coded thresholds (which work for stable normal distributions) are likely to be placed incorrectly.
A better approach is a dynamic threshold that self-adjusts to a percentile of the distribution of models released each year, combined with a risk index of multiple metrics rather than compute alone.
Governments should be transparent about which risks compute thresholds aim to mitigate and where they allocate limited resources, given a shortage of technical AI staff in government.
methods: Conceptual/argumentative policy essay analyzing the rationale and limitations of compute thresholds, framed around the question of whether 'bigger is always better' in AI
Literature synthesis on the relationship between compute and performance (data quality, optimization, architecture) to argue smaller models are becoming more performant
Empirical illustration using Open LLM Leaderboard data: plotting best daily models 13B or smaller over time and large (>13B) models outperformed by small models
Empirical illustration using Epoch AI database to show FLOP requirements differ across modalities and that model-attribute distributions are non-normal/skewed

Identification of specification loopholes in FLOP as a metric (inference-time compute, model lifecycle, MoE/ensembles, system-level risk, modality differences, quantization, theoretical vs practical FLOP)
Comparative analysis of scaling-laws literature to assess the track record of predicting downstream capability emergence with scale
Policy proposal: dynamic percentile-based thresholds and a risk index of multiple metrics, drawing on analogies from medicine, finance, and poverty measurement

members.title: Can there be responsible AI without AI liability? Incentivizing generative AI safety through ex-post tort liability under the EU AI liability directive
AI and Global Governance: Modalities, Rationales, Tensions
key_claims: AI has become a loose umbrella term, and the article is concerned less with defining AI than with which technologies and practices are proposed to be governed; speculative AGI/existential risk discussions are out of scope.

Governance modalities can be organized as ideal-type categories: ethical codes and councils, industry governance, contracts and licensing, standards, international agreements, and converging/extraterritorial domestic regulation.
AI ethics principles and councils have largely been vague, unenforceable, and have served predominantly to forestall regulatory action by firms ('ethics' as the new 'industry self-regulation').

A small number of firms control the physical, epistemic, and informational resources/bottlenecks needed to train AI systems, giving them outsized governance power, including via platform/as-a-service distribution.

Contractual and licensing approaches (e.g., RAIL behavioural-use restrictions on Stable Diffusion) attempt private transnational governance, but enforcement is limited because only copyright holders can enforce the license.
Standards bodies (IEEE P70xx, ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 42) empower well-resourced incumbents and bake value-laden, often proprietary policy decisions into technical standards.
Intergovernmental principles (OECD, UNESCO, G20) largely do not differ significantly from industry documents or interests, and digital power/competition is kept off the table.
The EU has emerged as a key player whose draft AI Act and other instruments produce transnational/extraterritorial impact via the harmonization of standards.

The global governance of AI is a contested concept currently substantially driven by industry interests, and framing issues as technological tends to lead to technological solutions that benefit technology firms.
Global South / Global Majority stakeholders face a 'paradox of participation' with surface-level inclusion but without structural reforms or resources for meaningful involvement.
methods: Critical literature review drawing on AI governance, governance of computing, and broader regulation/governance scholarship
Construction of ideal-type categories of AI global governance modalities organized in rough order of increasing institutional complexity
Conceptual framing distinguishing governance by target: development, use, and infrastructures of AI
Analysis of rationales and tensions using global governance theory (e.g., race-to-the-bottom, postnormal science, framing/STS perspectives)

members.title: AI Governance in the Context of the EU AI Act
AI Governance and Governance in AI For our Cities: Opportunities and Safeguards in the Transforming Global Construction Paradigm
Explainability in AI Policies: A Critical Review of Communications, Reports, Regulations, and Standards in the EU, US, and UK
Governing intelligence: Singapore’s evolving AI governance framework
key_claims: Singapore is characterised as taking a quasi-regulatory (soft-law), pro-business, tech-optimistic approach emphasising consensus-building and voluntary frameworks rather than horizontal hard regulation

Singapore was an early mover in AI governance, launching the IMDA Model Framework (Asia's first such framework) in 2019 and the world's first AI Governance Testing Framework and Toolkit, AI Verify, in 2022
Singapore has not enacted any general law specifically regulating AI and is not expected to introduce horizontal AI legislation soon, relying instead on general law, sectoral instruments and soft law
The GenAI-specific Model Framework sets out nine dimensions and reflects multi-layered risk management, while its necessity somewhat undermines the generality of the original Model Framework

Under the H-GenAIGF comparison, Singapore is classified as a mixed (risk-principle-based) model with strong coverage in some processes but partial coverage or gaps in others such as upholding user rights and managing distribution/access control
Singapore's approach has influenced the region, notably the 2024 ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics, which is consistent with the Model Framework and shares a risk-principle-based approach
methods: qualitative legal-policy document analysis
comparative governance analysis
case study
regulatory taxonomy/spectrum classification
application of comparative framework (H-GenAIGF)

members.title: The Dark Sides of Artificial Intelligence: An Integrated AI Governance Framework for Public Administration
Nascent regulatory sandbox frameworks for AI in Israel
key_claims: Israel adopts sector-specific regulatory sandboxes as experimental mechanisms to balance innovation with public interest concerns, preferring to adapt existing regulatory structures rather than create comprehensive AI-specific governance.

Israel's AV regulatory sandbox (2022 Traffic Ordinance Amendment No. 130) grants exemptions from traffic regulations (e.g., steering-wheel control under Regulation 28, international-standards compliance under Regulation 282) while maintaining safety oversight via control centers and incident reporting.

The proposed fintech sandbox uses a five-member multi-regulator committee and a dual-track (licensing and oversight) system for regulatory relief, but its multi-regulator structure may constrain regulatory agility and import inter-agency tensions.

The January 2025 general regulatory sandbox legislative guidelines establish a technology-neutral four-phase lifecycle framework (preliminary phase, experiment plan, experiment, ex post facto analysis).
The sector-specific approach facilitates targeted innovation but may inadequately address broader AI governance concerns such as algorithmic accountability and human oversight.
Reverse sandboxes are proposed as a way for regulators to proactively examine risks of emerging technologies and develop constraints, moving beyond merely granting regulatory easements.
Of the developments examined, only AV regulation has been implemented; the fintech sandbox remains at the bill stage and the legislative guidelines are untested in practice.
methods: qualitative case study
doctrinal legal analysis
policy document analysis
comparative regulatory analysis

members.title: Toward AI Governance: Identifying Best Practices and Potential Barriers and Outcomes
key_claims: AI governance is decomposed into structural, procedural, and relational practices, used as the main dimensions to explain how to govern AI and boost firm performance
AI was found most helpful for reducing maintenance costs, increasing flexibility and robustness of the development process, improving confidence in results/products, and gaining a competitive edge
Domain experts were involved in all development phases and led projects as project managers to ensure quality
Establishing an AI culture through training was difficult because employees feared losing their position to automation, distrusted outputs, and misunderstood AI capabilities
Firms preferred to build intelligence on top of external cloud/AI platforms rather than buy external solutions, to keep domain knowledge in-house and maintain competitive advantage

The proposed model identifies enablers (existing AI culture and architecture) and inhibitors (legal constraints, domain challenges, high development costs, AI-phobia), with outcomes of competitive advantage, cost reduction, and dependable AI systems
AI governance is multi-faceted, spans multiple levels (personal to organizational), and has a temporal angle since different concerns emerge at different phases of AI projects
AI lacks the ability to make decisions in specific contexts, so a manager must employ intuition to reconcile the choices provided by AI
methods: Exploratory comparative multi-case study of three firms in the energy sector in Norway
Semi-structured interviews with 15 respondents (domain and technical experts) from business and IT departments, recorded via Zoom and transcribed verbatim using Otter AI
Use of secondary data sources (annual reports, internal/public documents) for triangulation and validation
Narrative analysis with open and axial coding in NVivo, conducted independently by three authors across three iterations
Structural, procedural and relational governance dimensions used as the main analytic framework, plus cross-case (between-case) analysis

members.title: A Multilevel Framework for AI Governance
Review: AI Governance through Markets
Putting AI Ethics into Practice: The Hourglass Model of Organizational AI Governance
key_claims: The paper's central contribution is integrating AI governance layers, components, and literature into a single integrated model of organizational AI governance, visualized as an hourglass with three layers: environmental requirements, organizational practices and capabilities, and operational governance of AI systems

The hourglass metaphor captures the top-down flow/translation of governance requirements (regulatory, self-regulatory, stakeholder inputs) from the environmental layer through the organizational layer into operational AI system practices, plus bottom-up information flow

The environmental layer comprises three types of requirements ordered from most to least binding: hard law (normative regulation), principles and guidelines (self-regulation), and stakeholder pressure
The organizational layer comprises two key themes: strategic alignment and value alignment

The AI system (operational) layer has eight governance components: AI system, Algorithms, Data operations, Risk and impacts, Transparency/explainability/contestability, Accountability and ownership, Development and operations, and Compliance, decomposed into 67 tasks

Operational governance processes are tied to AI system life cycles so governance applies throughout the system's life span; six of the eight components are structurally similar (spanning design, verification, deployment, monitoring) while accountability and development operations are more front-heavy

The framework emphasizes the systemic, multilayered, and multi-stakeholder nature of AI governance and is designed to help organizations align with the forthcoming EU AI Act, especially in high-risk application areas
methods: conceptual framework development
design science / IT artifact conceptualization
industry co-development and case testing
regulatory cross-checking against EU AI Act
life-cycle process mapping (OECD model)

members.title: Operational responsibility in AI governance: a user-centric liability framework
key_claims: AI systems should be treated as tools/instruments whose outputs remain the responsibility of human operators (deployers) rather than developers ('user-centric governance')
Three principles - proximity, control, and expertise - justify placing primary responsibility with those who deploy AI rather than those who develop it
Developer-centric liability faces a fundamental attribution problem: tracing harms back to specific design choices is often infeasible, worsening as systems become more advanced
Placing accountability with deployers promotes public trust, preserves democratic accountability, and counters power asymmetries
For black-box/API deployments where deployer control is reduced, deployer obligations should intensify as control decreases while provider disclosure obligations increase ('distributed yet centered')
The framework operates within, not against, existing producer-liability architectures such as the EU Product Liability Directive, and aligns with EU AI Act deployer obligations (Articles 26-27)
Recent cases (Moffatt v. Air Canada 2024; Mata v. Avianca 2023) show courts treating AI as tools whose human deployers bear responsibility
methods: Conceptual/normative legal-philosophical argument drawing on tort law, agency law, and philosophy of technology to frame AI as an instrument/tool whose outputs are the operator's responsibility
Articulation of three justificatory principles (proximity, control, expertise) for user-centric governance, supplemented by law-and-economics efficiency analysis
A 'spectrum approach' calibrating deployer obligations to degree of control, with enhanced provider disclosure compensating for reduced deployer visibility in black-box/API deployments
Comparative legal/regulatory analysis of frameworks (EU AI Act, EU Product Liability Directive, Colorado AI Act, China's Interim Measures, Singapore Model AI Governance Framework, OECD AI Principles)
Distinguishing four differentiated responsibility types (causal, moral, role, legal) to articulate 'distributed yet centered' / 'distributed responsibility without distribution of accountability'

Proposed implementation mechanisms: adapted 'reasonable AI deployer' care standards, a safe harbor structure with triggering/loss conditions, disclosure/documentation requirements, organizational accountability structures, and AI literacy/competence programs

members.title: Governance of Generative AI
The diffuse void: algorithmic safety and the disappearance of judgment
key_claims: Contemporary safety mechanisms (red-teaming, toxicity scoring, RLHF) produce a crisis in the appearance of judgment, reorganizing decisions into continuous probabilistic optimization in which power operates without actors who appear publicly as authors of specific outcomes

RLHF restructures human evaluators as 'sensors' generating preference signals aggregated into a reward model rather than as moral agents exercising judgment, washing out the individual human act through aggregation

The reward model functions as a statistical proxy for normativity that reshapes probability space rather than issuing a binding prohibition, so the system cannot disobey or decide and what appears as obedience is merely successful convergence
First-person model refusals ('I cannot help') simulate a moral stance while masking the absence of a responsible subject, the paradigmatic expression of the diffuse void
Auditability substitutes for responsibility: governance artifacts like the GPT-4 System Card document the 'what' of behavior while maintaining opacity regarding the 'who' of authorization

The diffuse void is not a technical necessity of machine learning but an institutional choice of the proprietary safety regime, since open-source projects (e.g., EleutherAI, LAION) operate with named maintainers
The EU AI Act's 'meaningful human control' (Articles 14 and 29) conflates supervision with judgment, leaving the human verifying the slide rather than executing the cut
Responsibility can only appear at discrete infrastructural release points (model deployment, API publication) where probabilistic processes crystallize into institutional authorization decisions

Authorization tokens (cryptographic signatures by a named human agent for significant deployments) could restore identifiable loci of responsibility by creating a point of public appearance, with institutional friction being a necessary feature rather than a side effect
methods: Theoretical/conceptual framework drawing on Hannah Arendt's account of judgment, action, behavior, and 'rule by nobody' to distinguish discrete acts of judgment from probabilistic optimization
Introduction of new conceptual constructs ('post-agential governance' defined via three criteria; the 'diffuse void'; 'Safety Industrial Complex')
Symptomatic reading / case-study analysis of governance artifacts, specifically the GPT-4 System Card and the Google Gemini image-generation controversy
Phenomenological reconstruction of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), including the reward model and the phenomenology of refusal
Normative/institutional proposal of 'authorization tokens' (cryptographic signatures by named human agents at deployment) drawing analogy to software supply-chain signing

members.title: Evolving AI Risk Management: A Maturity Model based on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
key_claims: Despite many AI ethics frameworks and tools, organizations lag behind recommended best practices; e.g., in 2022 only 17% of companies reported working to mitigate fairness and bias issues, and only small fractions reported data/model documentation (9%) or maintaining an incident log (2%).

Basing the maturity model on the widely accepted NIST AI RMF avoids the drawbacks of bespoke frameworks (reinventing terminology, hindering benchmarking, and a political undertone), and facilitates comparability with industry standards and regulatory proposals.

Existing AI ethics maturity models are limited because they assume specific rigid trajectories toward good AI governance, whereas multiple legitimate trajectories exist depending on context (e.g., SMEs vs large corporations); the proposed model is open to multiple maturity trajectories.

The NIST AI RMF was chosen for its sociotechnical perspective on AI harm and its elevation of marginalized/impacted-stakeholder voices, and because the RMF naturally lends itself to a complementary maturity model that it does not itself provide.
The model defines 'robustness' as six interrelated ideals extracted from NIST implementation tiers: regular, systematic, trained personnel, sufficiently resourced, adaptive, and cross-functional.

Input diversity is included as a scoring metric (rather than only as statements) because it intersects most or all subcategories, reflecting how well a company solicits and uses feedback on its AI systems.
Aggregation by NIST pillar can expose systematic failures such as ethics washing (strong GOVERN but weak other pillars), while aggregation by responsibility dimension can reveal ignored risk areas.

In the case study, OpenAI's 'Approach to AI Safety' document scored 1 on the Measuring Risk topic (low coverage, low robustness, low input diversity), while Duolingo's 'English Test Responsible AI Standards' scored 3 (high coverage, medium robustness, low input diversity).
methods: Constructing a maturity model based on the NIST AI RMF rather than a bespoke framework, choosing the RMF over the EU AI Act for its applicability beyond high-risk systems and its voluntary, lifecycle-oriented, sociotechnical focus

A flexible questionnaire of 60 statements grouped into 9 topics, mapped to NIST AI RMF subcategories across the MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE, and GOVERN pillars, with three axes of flexibility: granularity, life-cycle stage (three stages), and multiplicity of AI systems

Scoring guidelines rating each statement 1-5 based on three metrics (coverage of RMF subcategories, robustness derived from NIST implementation tiers, and input diversity), each judged low/medium/high, combined via a points-based rule of thumb, with required evidence and rationale
Two modes of score aggregation: by NIST pillar (MAP/MEASURE/MANAGE/GOVERN) and by responsibility dimension (e.g., fairness, privacy, security), supporting multiple maturity trajectories

Design process combining an inductive conceptual step (this paper) with iterative author refinement and pilot-testing via consultations and dry runs with a convenience sample of AI stakeholders including NIST team members
A worked scoring case study applying the 'Measuring Risk' topic to public disclosures of OpenAI and Duolingo

members.title: Role of the state and responsibility in governing artificial intelligence: a comparative analysis of AI strategies
Regulatory Markets: The Future of AI Governance
key_claims: The authors propose 'regulatory markets,' in which governments require regulated targets to purchase regulatory services from government-licensed private regulators, as a solution that overcomes the limits of both command-and-control regulation and excessive delegation to industry

Governments set required outcomes (metric-based or principles-based), license and audit private regulators against those outcomes, and require targets to purchase regulatory services from licensed private regulators

Private regulators are expected to develop new 'regulatory technologies' (data-intensive, AI-based tools such as ML auditing, RLHF, and red-teaming), and driving investment/innovation in such technologies is a key reason to adopt regulatory markets

Reliance on standard-setting organizations (SSOs) is a 'false hope' for resolving the technical deficit because their frameworks supply procedural risk-management solutions, not technical detail, and they generate a democratic deficit

Regulatory markets address globalization/harmonization by letting private regulators operate globally and obtain licenses from multiple jurisdictions, reducing cross-jurisdictional compliance burdens while preserving national sovereignty over outcome goals
A regulatory markets approach does not require the US and China to agree on shared technical standards; each can license only regulators achieving its own outcomes

Red-teaming of frontier models (e.g., to reduce bioweapon misuse risk) is a concrete domain where independent licensed regulators could shift currently-internal corporate efforts to a sector accountable to both governments and developers
methods: Conceptual/normative policy proposal building on Hadfield's earlier 'regulatory markets' model and on regulatory intermediary theory (RIT) from Abbott, Levi-Faur, and Snidal

Comparative survey/analysis of the AI governance landscape circa 2025 across the EU (AI Act, DSA, DMA, GDPR), the US/UK (existing regulators plus voluntary NIST/ISO standards), and China (CAC regulations, generative AI Interim Measures)

Worked illustrative examples/case scenarios applying the model to specific domains (self-driving cars, banking, drones with facial recognition, red-teaming frontier models for bioweapon risk, and a global facial-recognition market)
Analysis of limitations and risks drawing on historical cautionary cases (credit rating agencies in the 2008 crisis, FAA oversight of the Boeing 737-MAX)

members.title: The UK’s AI Governance Strategy: Building Trust as Infrastructure
Portfolio Governance of AI for Australian Higher Education: With, Without and About AI
AI Governance in a Complex and Rapidly Changing Regulatory Landscape: A Global Perspective
key_claims: The authors argue that a new transnational legal architecture for AI is eventually bound to be created, similar to other fields, and that the question is one of timing rather than whether it will happen

An internationally coordinated response and a new global AI regulatory authority are necessary because of the borderless nature of AI, the inadequacy of purely national approaches, and competing state interests
International law currently lags behind in adopting appropriate rules for governing AI, and the international community has not yet provided an appropriate regulatory response to fast AI developments

A global AI authority should start with nonbinding instruments (recommendations, guidelines, standards) while building on the two binding instruments already adopted: the EU AI Act and the Council of Europe Framework Convention

International organizations cannot enforce treaties domestically; only states can, based on their consent, so a global authority's role would be to monitor whether governments implement their commitments and to provide guidance and expertise

Neither China nor the US appears to favor establishing a regulatory authority, preferring to give their companies a competitive edge, yet both participate in international discussions to influence regulation
Existing instruments such as the EU AI Act and the Council of Europe AI Convention should be further assessed and used as models for adopting international treaties
methods: Theoretical/conceptual framework centered on an AI regulatory authority that balances and organizes the roles, powers, and duties of global actors (states, international organizations, private companies, civil society), illustrated in Figure 1
Narrative literature review of scholarship on AI regulation, international law, and global governance

Doctrinal/qualitative analysis of existing legal initiatives and instruments (EU AI Act, Council of Europe Framework Convention, UNESCO recommendations, Chinese provisions, US executive orders/AI Bill of Rights)
Actor-by-actor analysis of stakeholder roles (states; natural persons; civil society organizations; corporate entities; international organizations)
Analysis of the two main functions of a proposed global AI authority: establishing international law and monitoring its domestic enforcement

members.title: Implementation of the EU AI act calls for interdisciplinary governance
AI Governance by Human Rights–Centered Design, Deliberation, and Oversight
Toward empowering AI governance with redress mechanisms
key_claims: Access to redress is, in fact, access to justice
Current AI governance frameworks fall short in protecting individuals' rights by focusing on ex-ante measures and neglecting ex-post redress
The redress process comprises four key steps, each presenting distinct challenges and requirements
Even the most stringent ex-ante measures may not entirely eliminate the risk of AI-related harms, making redress indispensable
The opacity of AI and the 'many hands problem' are two significant challenges in collecting evidence for redress
Neither the EU nor US framework has fully addressed the need for effective remedies for individuals harmed by AI
Monetary compensation alone fails to address systemic and structural issues of bias and inequality in AI systems
Effective design and enforcement of redress requires interdisciplinary research collaboration across law, social sciences and data science
methods: Conceptual/normative legal-policy analysis evaluating whether current AI governance provides adequate redress
Decomposition of the redress process into four steps with challenges examined for each
Doctrinal analysis of regulatory instruments (EU AI Act, AILD, PLD, GDPR, DSA, RAD)
Illustration via real-world case examples
Comparative analysis of EU vs US AI governance models
Stakeholder-targeted recommendations

members.title: The Challenge of European AI Risk Management: An Iron Cage for Water?
Institutionalised distrust and human oversight of artificial intelligence: towards a democratic design of AI governance under the European Union AI Act
key_claims: The AIA requires human oversight to be effective but provides little guidance on how to achieve effectiveness and leaves oversight obligations for AI developers underdefined

Human overseers are fallible: empirical research shows humans both over-rely (automation bias) and under-rely (algorithm aversion) on algorithmic advice and judge algorithmic accuracy poorly, so commanding oversight by law is no panacea

The paper introduces a novel taxonomy distinguishing first-degree overseers (counterfactual/constitutive influence on a decision) from second-degree overseers (no counterfactual influence, corrective/ex post roles such as audits, reviews, appeals)

Human oversight under the AIA is a shared responsibility between developers (who make AI oversee-able) and users/deployers (who execute oversight); some oversight obligations should fall on developers case-by-case for continuously learning AI systems

The paper formulates, for the first time applied to AI governance, six normative principles institutionalising distrust: justification; periodical mandates; collective decisions; limited competence of institutions; justiciability and accountability; transparency
Institutionalising distrust aims to increase the trustworthiness of AI governance and indirectly support the emergence of well-placed (justified) rather than naive trust in AI systems
The principles entail unavoidable trade-offs (e.g. periodical mandates can improve impartiality but undermine the competence that the justification principle requires)
methods: Conceptual/legal analysis surveying the emerging laws of human oversight, especially the EU AI Act (Commission proposal) and the Council and Parliament amendments, plus GDPR Article 22 and ISO/IEC technical standards

Construction of a novel two-dimensional taxonomy of human oversight roles based on whether human intervention has counterfactual influence (first-degree, constitutive) or not (second-degree, corrective), crossed with two challenges (lack of competence; wrong incentives) to form a two-by-two matrix of four areas of concern

Normative theory-building: drawing on democratic theory (Sztompka, Braithwaite) on institutionalised distrust to derive six design principles for human oversight and map their anticipated effects onto the four areas of concern

members.title: Multilevel oversight of AI systems in line with the AI Act
Generative AI and international standardization
key_claims: Standards complement regulation as frameworks for AI governance, codified in the EU as the New Legislative Framework since 2008 with predecessors going back to the 1980s, most recently applied to the EU AI Act

Under the New Legislative Framework regulation provides only high-level objectives while standardisation provides technical solutions, and harmonised standards are not mandatory but yield a presumption of conformity

Standardisation draws legitimacy from being consensus-based (close to unanimity) and from requiring inclusion of the full spectrum of affected stakeholders, though in practice this is tempered by unequal access to resources

Standardisation for generative AI is still in its infancy at both European and international levels because standardisation typically only begins once R&D reaches maturity and stability, which generative AI has not reached
The EU standardisation mandate (draft May 2022, formal May 2023) does not reference generative AI, and there has not been a single JTC21 work item addressing the specifics of generative AI

Generative AI standards development is hampered because key industry experts are employed by large players (OpenAI, Google, Mistral, Anthropic, Meta) focused on competition rather than standardisation

Most current generative AI governance activity is in the policy domain, including the EU AI Office Code of Practice on General Purpose AI, the Singapore Model AI Governance Framework, and the G7 Hiroshima process
Generative AI also drives the need for non-AI standards, especially in digital trust and digital identity, to keep the digital space resilient against deceptively real bots and AI-generated content
methods: Expository/practitioner analysis grounded in the author's experience as Chair of CEN-CENELEC JTC21, the committee developing harmonised standards for the EU AI Act
Descriptive review of the EU New Legislative Framework and key concepts (harmonised standards, presumption of conformity, legitimacy via stakeholders and consensus, top-down vs bottom-up)
Comparative survey of the state of generative AI standardisation across European (CEN-CENELEC JTC21), international (ISO/IEC JTC1/SC42), OECD, and national levels
Forward-looking enumeration of candidate topics for future generative AI standards and related non-AI standards (digital trust, digital identity)

members.title: Both eyes open: Vigilant Incentives help auditors improve AI safety
AI governance: themes, knowledge gaps and future agendas
Responsible artificial intelligence governance: A review and research framework
The Perilous State of AI Governance, June 2025
key_claims: The US faces a regulatory dilemma where too much regulation impedes AI development and too little exposes the world to excessive risk
Provably safe regulation of AGI is currently impossible because much about AGI behavior is unknown
The optimal approach is to apply the most advanced AI to construct the AI governance regime itself, termed recursive safety improvement, which must stay ahead of recursive self-improvement
Market mechanisms can provide efficient solutions but are imperfect and must coexist with slowly-evolving legal regimes
Congress should prevent fragmentation of the US into fifty different regulatory regimes to retain US leadership in AI
The bill's relevant section prohibits states and localities from regulating AI models, AI systems, or automated decision systems for 10 years
methods: Editorial argumentation / policy commentary on the state of US AI governance
Quotation and exegesis of legislative text from H.R.1 (the 'Big, Beautiful Bill'), including its 10-year state AI moratorium, federal IT modernization mandate, and statutory definitions
Proposal of 'recursive safety improvement' as a conceptual approach to building an evolving AI governance regime

members.title: Structuring AI Risk Management Framework: EU AI Act FRIA, GDPR DPIA and ISO 42001/23894
Frontrunner model for responsible AI governance in the public sector: the Dutch perspective
key_claims: The Netherlands is the frontrunner in AI governance models in the public sector, scoring first in the Global Index on Responsible AI, with its highest score for the 'government actions' pillar.

The Dutch Algorithm Register publishes algorithms used by public authorities, containing 488 entries (as of September 2024) from 330 authorities, structured into general information, responsible use, and processing categories.

The Algorithm Framework (Algoritmekader) transposes legislative AI texts into actionable information and adds a governance layer, but its complexity makes it mainly an instrument for public entities and specialists rather than end users.
Transparency and explainability are predictors of AI acceptance, and both are addressed by the two instruments analysed.
The AI Act is a risk-centred, hybrid legislation combining product safety and human rights approaches, but accurately classifying systems as high/medium risk is not straightforward in practice.

Of the algorithms currently in the Dutch register only 24 are high-risk, indicating public authorities take a rather cautious approach to publishing, with compulsory registration of high-risk algorithms planned from 2025.
Early adopters and frontrunners carry a responsibility because they shape future behaviour and become examples to be analysed for lessons of success or failure.
Increasing transparency can become counterintuitive for public authorities because publishing more information about high-risk systems can lead to vulnerability disclosure and risk.
methods: Qualitative case-study analysis of the Netherlands as the frontrunner in responsible AI governance, focused on the delegation acceptance perspective
Analysis of two Dutch open instruments: the public Algorithm Register (algoritmes.overheid.nl) and the Algorithm Framework (Algoritmekader)
Application of three theoretical lenses from prior literature (user-centric, delegation acceptance, societal adoption acceptance) and Hofstede cultural dimensions to interpret AI acceptance
Illustrative analysis of selected registered algorithms (e.g., automatic ID document check / face recognition, the Schengen visa processing algorithm KVV) to examine risk management and transparency
Risk management analysis mapping the AI Act's risk-based approach (product safety plus human rights framework) onto the Dutch instruments

members.title: Challenges and best practices in corporate AI governance: Lessons from the biopharmaceutical industry
key_claims: Defining and communicating ethical principles is a crucial first step toward implementing effective AI governance, but principles alone cannot ensure AI systems are designed and used ethically.

AstraZeneca's board published a set of Principles for Ethical Data and AI in November 2020 stating that AI use should be private and secure, explainable and transparent, fair, accountable, human-centric, and socially beneficial.
Organizations face four main implementation challenges: balancing interests (risk management vs innovation), defining 'AI' (scope), harmonizing standards, and measuring results.

Four transferable best practices are: build on existing policies and governance structures; use pragmatic and action-oriented terminology; focus on risk management in development and procurement; and empower employees through continuous education and change management.

The pharmaceutical industry is well-positioned to pioneer the operationalization of AI governance because of its history with sensitive data, its operation under laws and trust, and strong incentives given over $200 bn spent on pharmaceutical R&D yearly.

AstraZeneca launched four enterprise-wide initiatives: overarching compliance/guidance documents, a Responsible AI playbook, an internal Responsible AI Consultancy Service and AI resolution Board, and an externally-conducted AI audit.

Rather than defining AI precisely, AstraZeneca adopted a risk-based approach classifying systems as low-, medium- or high-risk with proportionate governance requirements, following the European Commission.
The most important step toward good corporate AI governance is to ensure procedural regularity and transparency, interlinking existing structures, tools and methods rather than inventing new ones.
methods: Case study / perspective drawing on the authors' first-hand experience guiding and coordinating the rollout of AI governance within AstraZeneca over a 12-month period

Participant observation and documentation: LF and JM observed and documented AstraZeneca's internal AI governance activities over two years (Q3 2020 to Q3 2022), recording challenges and best practices
Distillation of generalizable best practices from the observed organizational challenges and lessons learned

members.title: Governance Considerations of Adversarial Attacks on AI Systems
key_claims: Adversarial attacks deliberately manipulate AI system input data to mislead the system and produce inaccurate outputs, presenting security breaches and privacy violations
Adversarial attacks can undermine critical AI applications such as facial recognition and natural language processing, causing privacy violations, biased outcomes, and eroding public trust

The paper advocates for robust governance frameworks encompassing risk management, oversight, and legislative measures that prioritize confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA) of AI technologies
Mitigation strategies include data sanitization, continuous monitoring, model training, and proactive adversarial training to make models more resistant to attacks

Accountability among developers and researchers, transparency, and fairness are emphasized, and integrating legislative frameworks into AI development standards can enhance security and foster public trust

The paper proposes an integrated AI security governance model comprising seven components: risk management governance, leadership and oversight, development and deployment, AI regulations, user awareness, incident response, and continuous monitoring
Existing AI security frameworks (NIST AI RMF, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, Google SAIF, NCSC guidelines) provide a foundation but this area needs more research
methods: Conceptual / narrative review of the nature of adversarial attacks on AI systems and their threat vectors, drawing on industry and government sources (e.g., OWASP, NIST, vendor reports)

Taxonomy-style cataloguing of adversarial attack types and AI model vulnerabilities (prompt injection, insecure output handling, data poisoning, model denial of service, supply chain vulnerabilities, sensitive information disclosure, insecure plugin design, excessive agency, overreliance, model theft, black-box attacks)
Use of real-world case scenarios (autonomous vehicles, medical imaging, facial recognition glasses, Microsoft Tay chatbot) to illustrate impacts and implications
Review of existing AI security governance frameworks and standards (NIST AI RMF, OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, Google SAIF, NCSC guidelines, universal cyber governance model)
Proposal of an integrated AI security governance model with seven components, presented as Figure 1, adapting the NIST AI Risk Management Framework

On mapping values in AI Governance
AI-Mediated Public Decision-Making and Democratic Exclusion: Governance Risks and Accountability Frameworks
key_claims: Existing regulatory approaches remain oriented toward evaluating system performance rather than transformations in governance architecture.

Algorithmic governance transforms the institutional terrain on which democratic inclusion is realised, relocating decision-making from visible adjudication to less visible layers of system design and data processing.
Conceptualising AI as governance infrastructure shifts the analytical focus from individual decisions to the institutional environments in which decisions are produced.
An infrastructural perspective complements compliance-based frameworks by introducing an additional evaluative layer focused on institutional design.

comparative institutional analysis

members.title: Defining organizational AI governance
key_claims: AI governance is defined as a system of rules, practices, processes, and technological tools employed to ensure an organization's use of AI aligns with its strategies, objectives, and values, fulfills legal requirements, and meets principles of ethical AI followed by the organization
AI governance is positioned as a subset of corporate governance and IT governance and in partial overlap with data governance
AI systems should initially be viewed as special cases of IT systems requiring distinct governance tools, and may eventually be subsumed under IT governance as the field matures
Data governance is necessary but not sufficient for effective AI governance because data is only one element of algorithmic systems
Effective AI governance should be parsimonious, building on other governance areas and avoiding duplicated processes
The proposed definition incorporates technological tools to highlight that AI governance involves both human and technological components, and addresses the entire AI system life cycle
methods: Conceptual/synthesizing definition development: drawing on prior scholarly work on AI ethics and governance to propose a definition of AI governance at the organizational level
Conceptual positioning: situating AI governance relative to corporate governance, IT governance, and data governance using a figure (Fig. 1) and a comparative table (Table 1)
Literature review and synthesis of existing AI governance, corporate governance, IT governance, and data governance definitions to derive constituent elements

members.title: Transfeminist AI governance
key_claims: Large-scale AI governance systems structurally prioritize the needs of industry over marginalized communities, limiting governance through power imbalances and exclusionary norms

AI governance frequently proves ineffective at preventing harm because studies, practices, and systems of AI governance are limited by various forms of power relations (resource dependencies, rule-making, norms of inclusion)
Canadian federal and provincial AI governance initiatives prioritize industry development, innovation, and economic growth over protections for vulnerable groups, workers, and the environment
Top-down AI governance is insufficient and bottom-up AI governance led by communities, workers, and civil society is necessary to enact transfeminist principles
Re-grounding AI governance in transfeminist ethical principles (transformative change, fluidity, community, resistance) can help address governance limitations

A preliminary transfeminist agenda proposes three parallel actions: expand the scope of AI and AI governance, oppose exclusionary AI governance systems, and co-create bottom-up systems to reduce dependency on industry and the state
AI and data-intensive technologies cause trans communities physical, psychological, social, political, and economic harms, and state power is sometimes actively exercised to harm trans people
methods: Develops 'transfeminist AI governance' grounded in trans and feminist theories of ethics, defined as the application of transfeminist ethical principles to the study and practice of AI governance, operationalized via a six-point 'transfeminist lens'
Applies a critical self-reflexivity methodology (the 4Rs: retrospection, representation, review, reinterpretation) to retroactively reinterpret findings from three prior empirical studies
Study 1: integrative review of 67 sources on ethical and governance issues in global AI value chains, developing a theoretical framework of benefit/harm co-creation
Study 2: semi-systematic review and content analysis of documentation from 84 federal and provincial AI governance initiatives in Canada (2017-2022)
Study 3: content analysis and service systems analysis of 20 interviews with government leaders and subject matter experts about Canada's national AI governance system
Introduces 'AI countergovernance' as a conceptual/practical framework synthesizing four real-world cases of collective organizing against state-led and industry-led AI governance systems

Outsider Oversight: Designing a Third Party Audit Ecosystem for AI Governance
Destined for Balance? Centralized and Decentralized Approaches to AI Governance
key_claims: States with high income and strong R&D capacity tend to adopt a more decentralized AI governance approach (supports H2a).
States with high income but weak R&D capacity tend to adopt a more centralized AI governance approach (supports H2b).
States with weak R&D capacity and high ethical risk level adopt a more centralized approach to incentivize innovation and control risks.
Per capita GNI is the only necessary condition for a decentralized AI governance approach, with coverage 0.543, confirming H1.
The influence of income level and R&D capacity outweighs the influence of ethical risk level on governance choices.
A high level of ethical risk positively influences a centralized governance approach, contrary to H3b, and H3a was not verified.
Deviant cases (Singapore, France) suggest a balanced governance approach can facilitate AI innovation while safeguarding human rights and managing risk.
methods: Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) combining case-oriented qualitative and variable-oriented quantitative methods on eight states (US, China, Germany, France, Singapore, India, Brazil, Russia)

Construction of a multi-dimensional dependent variable (degree of centralization/decentralization) measured via central-government documents, local AI policies, non-state actor scores, and transparency/auditability indicators, preprocessed with entropy weight and linear weighted sum methods
Calibration of conditions into fuzzy membership sets using three-value and four-value anchoring methods, including an indirect fractional-logit calibration for per capita GNI
Necessary-condition analysis (consistency threshold 0.9, coverage threshold 0.5) and sufficient-condition (truth table) analysis producing complex, intermediate, and parsimonious solutions
Case studies triangulating fsQCA sufficient pathways with policy-document evidence and contextualizing deviant cases
Robustness check resetting the consistency threshold to 0.85

members.title: AI policy in healthcare: a checklist-based methodology for structured implementation
key_claims: The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), effective 2025, imposes binding obligations on healthcare organizations, making a structured AI approach a regulatory obligation rather than merely advisable
From February 2, 2025 the AI Act mandates AI literacy/training for staff interacting with AI systems, requiring tiered training (basic, advanced, ongoing) with systematic documentation

The proposed methodology helps healthcare professionals ask the right questions rather than providing ready-made answers, allowing operational flexibility that adapts to evolving technology and regulation

The checklist's clinical and technical validation section addresses clinical effectiveness, technical robustness, MDR compliance, GDPR adherence, and post-deployment monitoring; the governance and compliance section addresses AI Act conformity, accountability, human oversight, traceability, AI literacy, and audits/updates
The AI Act applies in healthcare both to organizations that develop AI systems (providers) and those that use them (deployers)
The checklist has the potential to be incorporated into an AI policy to support assessment of AI systems
methods: A checklist-based methodology that generates critical evaluative questions (guiding questions rather than rigid prescriptive rules) to assess AI systems' appropriateness, reliability, and legal/ethical implications
A domain-specific operational checklist with two integrated sections/domains: clinical and technical validation, and governance and compliance
Mapping the checklist content to EU AI Act, MDR, and GDPR compliance requirements, plus AI literacy/training planning

members.title: Designing Ethical AI Governance for Contract Management Systems in International Procurement Frameworks
key_claims: Core ethical principles for AI in contract management are accountability, fairness, transparency, privacy, and human autonomy
Human-in-the-loop (HITL) mechanisms are critical safeguards ensuring algorithmic outputs are reviewed and validated by qualified personnel before binding decisions
Algorithmic bias, discrimination, and lack of explainability are major risks of automating contract management, turning systems into black boxes that threaten due process and accountability
Multilateral procurement frameworks (WTO, UNCITRAL, OECD) predate AI adoption and lack explicit provisions for algorithmic transparency, model bias, or AI accountability, creating a normative vacuum
Cross-border AI deployment introduces ethical dilemmas including algorithmic impartiality, conflicting legal doctrines, weak auditability, and power asymmetries between countries or vendors
Digital sovereignty and data jurisdiction conflicts arise when AI contract systems are hosted on foreign cloud platforms or trained on cross-border datasets

Accountability in AI-based contract enforcement becomes diffused across developers, data scientists, procurement officers, and system integrators, requiring layered accountability protocols and audit trails

The paper recommends risk-based AI classification, codifying fairness/transparency/accountability into procurement law, mandatory impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes, and a global registry of AI procurement tools
Ethical AI performance should be evaluated using multidimensional metrics for fairness, transparency, accountability, and inclusion beyond accuracy or efficiency
Global harmonization should mean coordinated diversity (common principles with context-specific adaptations) rather than uniformity, supported by technologies like blockchain and federated learning
methods: Qualitative synthesis of interdisciplinary literature, policy documents, and case studies
Comparative analysis of governance models across jurisdictions
Thematic coding of policy guidelines from OECD, UNCITRAL, and regional trade bodies
Case study analysis of multilateral, corporate, and public-sector procurement

members.title: The Bureaucratic Challenge to AI Governance: An Empirical Assessment of Implementation at U.S. Federal Agencies
From Structured Compute To Governed Infrastructure
European artificial intelligence policy as digital single market making
key_claims: Single market integration is a fundamental but overlooked engine and structuring principle of new EU AI regulation
Removing barriers to competition and the free flow of data, and securing ethical and responsible AI, are seen as compatible and even mutually reinforcing under this principle

Markets and ethics are deeply entangled and conceptually inseparable problems rather than conflicting imaginaries; market integration is cast in ethical terms while ethics are conceived in market terms

Data is conceptualized as the new 'raw material' for the digital age, creating a paradox where it is simultaneously a property-commodity and a public infrastructure, with risk of big tech 'gatekeepers' monopolizing access
EU AI regulation is motivated by the impending 'fragmentation' of the Single Market resulting from asymmetric and uncoordinated national policies
Key EU AI legislative proposals consistently find their legal basis in Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union concerning the Internal Market

The new legal concept of 'gatekeeper' in the Digital Markets Act revises the existing competition framework to tackle big tech, which is simultaneously a condition for and a barrier to competition (a paradox)
Quantitatively, mentions of AI surged from almost none around 2016/2017, with AI associated more frequently with 'market', 'infrastructure' and 'Single Market' than with 'ethics' and 'vision'

members.title: An Action-Oriented AI Policy Toolkit for Technology Audits by Community Advocates and Activists
Better together? Human oversight as means to achieve fairness in the European AI Act governance
key_claims: Human oversight relates to fairness in three non-exclusive normative ways: mitigating AI bias (non-discrimination), placing liable natural persons over non-liable AI systems (accountability), and introducing empathy/contextual sensitivity into decision-making.

The AI Act mentions fairness only five times across its 144 pages and does not define it in the legally binding part; recital 27 defines fairness as inclusion, equal access, gender equality, cultural diversity and lack of discriminatory impacts and biases.

The AIA establishes a threefold oversight structure distributed among providers, deployers and appointed overseers, but places the technical burden of identifying oversight measures entirely on the provider while treating the deployer as a mere executor.

Providers lack visibility into specific deployment contexts and the AIA imposes no cooperation obligation between providers and deployers, creating gaps in addressing context-specific biases that compromise non-discrimination.

Human oversight required by the AIA is prominently technical in nature, with organizational oversight measures not explicitly mentioned, which undermines accountability by burdening the appointed overseers.

The AIA does not consider the possible side-effects of transparency and explainability (such as over-reliance/automation bias) or the hand-off problem, which can compromise the empathy dimension of fairness.
The AIA does not safeguard the duration of human intervention; lack of adequate time can render human oversight merely symbolic, affecting non-discrimination and empathy.

The CJEU established a link between fairness and meaningful human intervention in automated decision-making (Schufa and PNR cases), where human involvement must be significant and capable of influencing the outcome.
Human oversight is not a panacea for AI's flaws, facing challenges of meaningfulness, feasibility and effectiveness, but remains a crucial component of AI governance.

The article makes two novel contributions: describing three fairness-related normative goals for human oversight, and showing how the AIA only partially creates a structure that materializes fairness as non-discrimination, accountability and empathy.
methods: Interdisciplinary literature review synthesizing technical, ethical and legal arguments to derive three normative claims linking human oversight to fairness
Doctrinal/critical legal analysis of the EU AI Act (notably Article 14 and related provisions) against the three fairness dimensions
Structured analysis of human oversight under the AIA using a who/what/how/when framing
Comparative legal analysis drawing on the GDPR (Article 22, Recital 71), the Article 29 Working Party guidance, and CJEU case law (Schufa C-634/21; PNR C-817/19)

key_claims: There is currently no specific/comprehensive law in Malaysia governing AI, so AI-related issues are controlled by existing laws, regulations, and industry standards
The requirement for a human creator in the Malaysian Copyright Act makes it highly improbable that copyright will apply to AI-generated content
Under Malaysian law AI systems lack legal personality and cannot satisfy the capacity-to-contract requirements of Section 11 of the Contracts Act 1950
Malaysia would benefit from an early lead in AI legislation, as only China and the EU have so far enacted such regulation while the USA and UK are progressing

members.title: Negative Human Rights as a Basis for Long-term AI Safety and Regulation
key_claims: Negative human rights can serve as a minimal set of principles that all AI systems should respect, forming a foundation for both international regulation and technical safety constraints, because they are general and already widely accepted

Defining rights operationally via the judgement of an adjudication system makes the otherwise abstract concept concrete and turns human rights compliance into a machine-learning-amenable task with the adjudication system as ground truth

The proposal restricts to negative rights (not positive rights) because negative rights protect an autonomous sphere from interference by any actor including AI, are less internationally controversial, and the state is the natural duty-bearer for positive rights

Human rights in law are largely relative legal principles handled via optimization/proportionality balancing with finite (though high) penalties, so absolute-rule paralysis under uncertainty is not a special problem; the right not to be tortured is a rare absolute right

Negative human rights are preferable to mandating full human values because an international overlapping/incompletely-theorized consensus is feasible on a rights subset but not on full, divergent human values
Negative human rights protection should be superior to other goals, acting as constraints within which the primary goal is pursued and taking precedence in case of conflict
Compared with the default patchwork of narrower rules, a human-rights-based framework offers more general guidance with a better chance of scaling robustly into unforeseen future situations
methods: Drawing on legal theory and legal realism to define human rights operationally: a behaviour is in accordance with human rights if a particular adjudication system would judge it to be so

Restricting the proposal to a subset of negative human rights for which there is wide international (overlapping/incompletely-theorized) consensus, e.g. right to life, security of person, property, not to be tortured

Framing human rights compliance as a machine learning task: a binary/real-valued risk-recognition classifier outputting an expected penalty for rights violation, treated as a supervised-learning black box
Specifying inputs (belief state and action representations) on a generality spectrum from system-specific representations to general natural-language court-style representations

Enumerating learning sources: direct RL feedback, case law, statutory law/regulations, other legal literature, formal constraints, observation of human behaviour (inverse RL), and large-scale text corpora/language models

Defining integration desiderata (Human Rights Primacy, No Adversarial Optimization, Conservatism with respect to Uncertainty) and discussing bounding primary reward, pessimism, and counterfactual-oracle-style methods to prevent specification gaming

An exploratory governance proposal: an international convention codifying protected rights plus a hierarchical adjudication system, national enforcement, and a private training ecosystem of safety providers under regulatory oversight

members.title: The crisis of the tripod of legal legitimacy: AI, governance and the shifting foundations of legitimacy
key_claims: AI systems do not merely support decision making but embed regulatory authority within their technical design, shaping behavior without democratic authorization
Legal legitimacy rests on three interdependent conditions conceptualized as the Tripod of Legal Legitimacy: legal certainty, accountability and enforceability
AI systems systematically undermine the tripod, producing 'legal displacement': the persistence of legal form without its underlying authority
Private regimes such as Meta's Oversight Board and OpenAI simulate legal form without legal authority
Across the AI-induced stages the Tripod is progressively eroded, with enforceability becoming symbolic rather than binding
Reconstructing legal authority requires institutional transformation rather than reliance on ethical frameworks or voluntary compliance
methods: Conceptual/normative-analytical legal analysis synthesizing doctrinal, institutional and regulatory developments, drawing on comparative public law and EU legal instruments rather than empirical datasets

Case-based comparative analysis of two emblematic public-law instruments (EU Digital Services Act and EU AI Act) against private governance regimes (Meta's Oversight Board and OpenAI's governance/safety protocols)

Development of a process-based model contrasting a Traditional Legal-Governance Framework with an AI-Induced Governance Displacement Framework to trace recursive regulatory feedback cycles

members.title: Bridging the gap: the case for an ‘Incompletely Theorized Agreement’ on AI policy
key_claims: The research community appears divided between those emphasizing near-term concerns and those focusing on long-term concerns and corresponding policy measures.

The principle of an 'incompletely theorized agreement', derived from constitutional law, can bridge underlying disagreements and provide philosophical foundations and historical precedent for cooperation between divergent communities.
Scholars working with near-term and long-term perspectives can converge and cooperate on selected mutually beneficial AI policy projects while maintaining their distinct perspectives.
Perceived differences between the communities may be overstated, and even if such differences exist they are not practically insurmountable.

Historical examples show that the structure of a field or community affects its members' ability to shape policy, and that collaboration yields significant benefit while fragmentation can harm policy impact.
There is a closing window of opportunity because the AI policy field will likely become progressively more rigid as framings, public perceptions, and stakeholder interests crystallize.
Incompletely theorized agreements allow a community to bypass or suspend intractable theoretical disagreement where there is an urgent need to address shared practical issues.
Incompletely theorized agreements have broad similarities with John Rawls's notion of an 'overlapping consensus'.
A community's influence on policymaking is significantly stronger if it acts as a united front rather than as scattered subgroups.
methods: Conceptual/argumentative analysis examining the alleged near-term/long-term 'gap' and the practical space for inter-community collaboration on AI policy

members.title: AI Governance Exploring Key Regulatory Approaches
key_claims: Increased AI capability and accessibility on consumer-grade equipment significantly raise the risks AI poses to society, motivating regulation.
Most key AI regulatory efforts have occurred within the past three years, and notable efforts have been made by the UK, EU, China, Brazil and Canada.
Except for China, no jurisdiction had yet finalised and enforced AI regulations at a national or international level; China enforced its algorithmic recommendation regulations in March 2022.

The EU's regulations are closest to being finalised, expected to be enforced in 2024, and will likely prove highly influential on AI regulations worldwide (notably inspiring Brazil and possibly Canada).
The UK's framework is principle-based with five key principles and aims to balance trust with promoting innovation, rather than focusing solely on trustworthiness.
The EU adopts a tiered, risk-based approach categorising AI into four risk levels (unacceptable, high, low, minimal) with maximum penalties up to 35 million euros or 7% of annual worldwide turnover.

China's regulations are distinctive: they are partly aimed at national security/content management and do not provide a general-purpose definition of AI, instead listing specific technological behaviours.
Brazil and Canada drew inspiration from the EU, using the OECD definition of AI and prioritising human rights, while Canada (like the UK) is principle-based.
The US has not proposed comprehensive federal AI regulations but issued an October 2023 executive order with eight guiding principles, suggesting federal regulation may eventually follow.

Open questions remain: enforcement at the individual/home-user level is unaddressed, financial penalties may fail as deterrents if noncompliance profits exceed fines, AI definitions trade breadth against clarity, and multiple regulations are likely to coexist rather than one becoming a global standard.
